speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 106(8), I have the honour of tabling, in both official languages, the Government's response to two petitions numbered as follows: 332-5372 and 332-5379.
[Editor's Note: See today's Votes and Proceedings.]

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 106 I have the honour and privilege to table a petition which has been certified correct as to form and content by the Clerk of Petitions. The petition is signed by a number of residents of northwestern Ontario in Thunder Bay, Marillo, Kaministiquia, South Gillies, Nolalu, and Kakabeka Falls.
These people petition the Parliament of Canada with regard to child care services. They point out that families throughout Canada need high quality, available, affordable child care services. They believe that the child care Bill which is currently before the other place is not in the best interests of young children, women, or families in Canada. The undersigned, your petitioners, humbly pray and call upon Parliament to withdraw the child care Bill forthwith.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR RETENTION OF TEN WEEK QUALIFYING PERIOD FOR UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also have the honour and the privilege of tabling a number of petitions, including several from the residents of St-Louis-de Kent, Jardineville, Rexton, Acadieville, St-Ignace, Tweedy Brook, Pointe-Sapin, Newcastle, St-Charles, Grande-Digue and Notre-Dame.
I have another petition from residents of Sackville, Dorchester, Upper Sackville, West Sackville and Jolicure.
Mr. Speaker, your petitioners deplore the Government's failure to act on the issue of unemployment insurance in New Brunswick. As you know, the eligible period was extended from 10 to 16 weeks. The situation is gradually getting worse. Your petitioners therefore humbly pray and ask Parliament to correct this situation and reinstate the 10-week eligible period for unemployment insurance.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 106 I have the honour and pleasure to present a petition on behalf of 44 petitioners of Edmonton. The petitioners, the undersigned residents of Canada, avail themselves of their ancient and undoubted right to present a grievance common to your petitioners in the certain assurance that this honourable House will provide a remedy.
They say that Canada is a nation of many cultures gathered and living in freedom and that in Eastern Europe there are still many nations of people dominated against their wills by oppressive Communist regimes. These nations are continually struggling against their oppressor to regain their rightful democratic freedoms.
Therefore, the undersigned humbly pray and call upon Parliament to recognize the struggle of these oppressed people and actively pursue a policy to alleviate their oppression through helpful programs and representations to the oppressive Soviet regime.
This petition is certified correct as to form.

Mr. Speaker, the second petition I have is also addressed to the Government of

Canada. The petitioners urge the Government to exert immediate pressure on the Polish Government to begin a dialogue on the authentic representative of the Polish workers, Solidarity, and not to use force in the current wave of strikes in Poland as an effort by the Polish people led by Solidarity to solve the country's problems without violence.
This petition is signed by 184 residents of Edmonton. This petition was not certified correct.

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of State and Minister of State (Treasury Board)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
subsubtopic: ALLEGED COERCION TO FALSIFY TRAVEL CLAIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Last Tuesday at this time I rose in the House in response to an article in The Ottawa Citizen dated September 20, 1988.
In that article a former employee alleged that during her brief term of employment from October, 1987 to February, 1988, she had been coerced into falsifying travel expenses. I indicated to the House that my staff and I were satisfied that there were no irregularities because we had conducted our own investigation when the matter was first brought to our attention on or about September 8, 1988.
Nevertheless, as a result of the newspaper article I immediately requested a full investigation of the allegations by the Privy Council Office. That investigation has been completed. Today I have been advised in a letter by the Privy Council Office that the travel expenditures during this period complied fully with the relevant regulations and guidelines and no irregularities were discovered.
This week has been most difficult for myself, my staff, and my family. On our behalf I want to thank those friend and foe who offered support and encouragement. I table herewith a copy of the letter received from the Privy Council Office.

Hon. Doug Lewis, for the Minister of Communications, moved that Bill C-136, an Act respecting broadcasting and to amend certain Acts in relation thereto and in relation to radiocommunication be read the third time and do pass.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of Labour):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today to rise in the House and speak to Bill C-136, which this Government sees as being vitally important to all Canadians.
Madam Speaker, over the years, and even more so in recent years, radio and televison have become an essential component, indeed the very framework of a society's cultural development. The latest figures indicate that in just one week, a typical Canadian listens to eighteen hours of radio and spends 24 hours watching tv. This shows how much these media have become a part of our lives. They provide a direct window on the world and affect and reflect our choices and our values.
The television landscape has become more complex in recent years, Madam Speaker. Before, it consisted basically of stations that transmitted signals and antennae that received them. Since then, both communications technology and the very nature of our society have changed significantly. Today, 78 per cent of Canadian homes are served by cable TV and can receive as many as 60 or 70 different channels. The possibilities in this area seem endless.

We know we will be unable to resist these changes, so it is important that we retain our jurisdiction in these areas and that the social and cultural objectives we have set are reaffirmed and protected.
The Caplan-Sauvageau task force spent several months looking for better ways to address these concerns. It travelled throughout Canada meeting with people who work in communications and with other Canadians who have an interest in this subject. The findings and recommendations of the task force were then closely reviewed by the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, which also engaged in extensive consultation with individuals and groups involved in radio and television.
The Bill we are considering today reflects many of the concerns raised during this three-year process.

The reason our communication policy is so important, may I remind you, Madam Speaker, is that it lies at the very heart of the concept of sovereignty. We think it is so fundamental that from the outset, we excluded our cultural industries and our
September 27, 1988

communications sector from the Free Trade Agreement with the United States.
This key aspect of our commitment is clearly written into Clause 3 of the Bill, which states:
The Canadian broadcasting system, operating primarily in the English and
French languages... provides, through its programming, a public service
essential to the maintenance and enhancement of national identity and cultural
sovereignty;
The connection that we make, Madam Speaker, between our broadcasting policy and our Canadian identity attests to the particular situation in which we find ourselves and which I mentioned earlier, that of a country that must continually strive to assert its national identity in a specific geographic and demographic context.

That identity is a dynamic thing. Since 1968, when the present Broadcasting Act was passed, much has happened which impacts on broadcasting. The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the changing role of women, a greater recognition of the particular contributions made by the French and English speaking communities, the richness of our multicultural diversity, and the recognition of the special place of aboriginal people in Canadian society are all changing how we approach broadcasting and what is expected of the medium. The pressure for legislation which recognizes this changed reality grows every day.
Canada is a much different country today, and Bill C-136 governing the broadcasting system reflects these changes. The existence of two official languages is more than just a constitutional reality. It pervades the entire broadcasting system. Bill C-136 specifically recognizes the existence of the two official languages and insists that they be reflected throughout the broadcasting system.
The CBC has particular responsibilities, as does the CRTC, in the application of its regulations.
[ Translation]
For this requirement that we have embodied into the law is not ideological but pragmatic. It is based on economic imperatives, on market realities, and the differences are glaringly obvious, Madam Speaker.
The first difference is that English television in this country suffers essentially from a lack of Canadian dramatic programming, especially in prime time.
The second is that although Canadian content standards are generally respected on French television, there is a problem of program quality related to budgets and production costs.
These different realities of English and French broadcasting, which are related to the very nature of Canada, had to be recognized, Madam Speaker. And I am particularly pleased that the Government of which I am part took the initiative. For the first time in a cultural Bill, these obvious realities are admitted; this is a tribute to the cultural reconciliation
Broadcasting Act
between Quebec and English Canada. I believe that we all have reasons to be proud of this.
Now, how will we deal with these two types of problems that I mentioned earlier? How will we encourage more Canadian content on English television and the development of French television? We have chosen several approaches that I would like to tell you about now, Madam Speaker.

I should make it clear at the outset that the Government never even considered limiting the access of Canadians to American programs. What we really want to ensure through a culturally active policy is that television interviewers have a Canadian alternative. We want foreign services introduced in Canada only in such a way that it strengthens existing and new Canadian services. This act gives the CRTC, for the first time, explicit powers to ensure that this will happen.
A common observation about English television in Canada is that Canadian content is particularly low in dramatic productions even though drama accounts for 70 per cent of television air time. This is due to the high costs of producing dramas and the attractiveness of American programs which are usually available to Canadian broadcasters at very low prices.
The strongest argument in favour of increasing the number of Canadian dramas on English language television in this country is that viewers prefer dramatic programs. However, popular shows of this type also help define a society by reflecting its choices and values and are probably the best way of getting people to think about who they are.
This legislation offers two methods of increasing the quantity and quality of Canadian programming, particularly dramatic programming in English. The first is by redefining the mandate of the CBC to make it clear that its function henceforth is to be the provision of distinctively Canadian programming in all program categories.

The Bill provides another incentive to increase the Canadian content of programming. English-language private broadcasters will have to meet certain objectives, depending on their size, situation and of course their resources. If they exceed these objectives, they will receive financial assistance from Telefilm. If they fail to meet the objectives, they will have to contribute to a development fund for the production of Telefilm's Canadian programs.

We realize that some private broadcasters have reservations about this matter. Our response has been and will continue to be that things cannot go on as they are. Broadcasting has always been one of the most prosperous industries in this country, but it has not contributed enough to the development of television that is truly Canadian. Broadcasters must realize that they have a responsibility to Canadians, a social and

September 27, 1988
Broadcasting Act
cultural responsibility that they cannot ignore. Granted, the prosperity I just mentioned is not always evenly distributed among broadcasting companies but we have taken this into account, establishing a system of contributions that is defined in terms of the revenue of each broadcaster.

I found the criticism of this provision of the Bill as voiced by Quebec broadcasters quite unreasonable. As I pointed out earlier, French-language television has always been remarkable for its responsible attitude to Canadian content, and therefore its artisans should not in any way feel threatened by the contribution proposal.
Madam Speaker, I would now like to touch on the double relationship to be established, under the proposed legislation, between Parliament and the institutions involved in broadcasting policy and Canadian telecommunications, namely the CRTC and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
As you know, Madam Speaker, the CRTC has always enjoyed enormous autonomy in carrying out its mandate, thus guaranteeing Canadians that their broadcasting system is not subject to unnecessary pressure.
However, a number of former presidents of the organization have deplored the absence of clear direction in the general orientation of our broadcasting policy. The Government wanted to correct this situation while at the same time leaving the CRTC the greatest possible leeway in the decision-making process. The approach was approved in the Sauvageau-Caplan Report and was also supported by the Standing Committee of this House.
Bill C-136 provides that the Government may give the CRTC general instructions regarding the objectives of the broadcasting policy. As for the Government's review authority, we have decided to restrict it to situations where these broad objectives were not met.
After examining the representations that were made, the Government also decided to relinquish its proposed authority to exempt certain categories of broadcasters from the legislation.
Madam Speaker, I firmly believe that we have here every possible guarantee that in future, the CRTC will be able to continue to carry out its mandate, undisturbed and fully autonomous, in the best interests of Canadians.

The commission itself, as well as certain other witnesses before the legislative committee, raised concerns that the new decision-making process, he who hears decides, and the greater emphasis on regional concerns, will lead to inconsistencies in CRTC decisions. It is the Government's belief that the legislation, including an amendment made at committee requiring panels to consult with the commission as a whole, provides the commission with ample means to avoid inconsistency. Any additional effort in this regard is more than
compensated for by greater responsibilities to regional concerns.

The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has always been the spearhead of broadcasting policy, in that it has paved the way, so to speak, for other broadcasters in the pursuit of certain objectives. Furthermore, it is the most important cultural instrument and the largest employer of Canadian artists. This perception of the CBC's role is not questioned, Madam Speaker. But for the first time, it is now backed up by a very clear provision concerning its independence. In this regard, I refer you, Madam Speaker, to Clause 45 of the Bill, which states:
The Corporation shall, in the pursuit of its objects and in the exercise of its powers, enjoy freedom of expression and journalistic, creative and programming independence.
Madam Speaker, I know that the President of the CBC expressed serious reservations about the structural reform proposed in the Bill. In particular, he feels that the decision to create a two-headed board of directors is likely to compromise the CBC's independence. With all due respect to him, I believe that the president's criticisms do not stand up to analysis.
The Government proposed the appointment of a chairman of the board and of a chief executive officer in order to rationalize the corporation's operations. This structural reform is accompanied by mechanisms to provide better control of the Corporation's financial operations.
What you must understand in this proposal, Madam Speaker, is that with nearly a billion dollars of public money invested in the corporation, it is essential for the trustees of these funds, namely the Government and Parliament, to be able to know exactly how this money is spent.
This does not show a desire to reduce the CBC's autonomy-the corporation's independence is very well guaranteed-but the need to ensure that the taxpayers' money is administered in the public interest.
Finally, Madam Speaker, I would like to comment briefly on the provisions of the Bill concerning the rapid evolution of broadcasting technology. The frequent technological changes of recent years have led to jurisdictional conflicts and quarrels that have cost a great deal of energy and have been detrimental to the public interest.
We must be glad that the legislation before us remains neutral in defining technology. Broadcasting is no longer defined in terms of the vehicle as such but of the content.
In addition to avoiding unnecessary and costly conflicts, this neutrality will allow distribution systems to develop at their own rate, in terms of the use of broadcasting technology, while the law still remains in effect.
So in summary, Madam Speaker, this is a piece of legislation that, besides being pragmatic, very clearly establishes a
September 27, 1988

set of essential principles that are in keeping with the nature of this country itself.
I see this legislation as a fundamental reform in the approach it proposes to our Canadian situation. Of course, Madam Speaker, the consultation process did not end when the Bill was tabled. Inevitably, with a Bill of this scope and complexity, which affects practically all Canadians, starting with our broadcasters, but also all those who see it as a tool that is indispensable to maintaining and enhancing their culture, we had a right to expect the legislative committee to do a very thorough job. We were not disappointed.
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) was admirable in that she managed to table a bill that would be able to meet the aspirations of Canadians in broadcasting, especially since the Bill has taken into account the constraints and challenges attendant on the expectations of the various social groups within our society, and this in the context of a rapidly expanding technology. That the Minister of Communications was able to achieve this in the past few weeks, through her own amendments and the amendments she approved among those suggested by Members of all Parties in this Elouse, clearly shows how intent she was on giving Canadians broadcasting legislation that would respond to their needs and expectations for many years to come.
Where the dangers of Government intervention loomed too large, the Minister did not hesitate to reduce that risk. Where measures might have been judged too weak to respond to the aspirations of a given group in our society, she made sure the text of the Bill was amended so as to remove any ambiguity about the Government's intentions in this respect.
In some cases, as with the provisions for educational broadcasting, for example, the complexity and jurisdictional delicacy of the subject matter have dictated that the substance of the measures be contained in the more flexible instrument of an Order in Council, with only brief mention in the legislation proper.

As a result of these amendments to a Bill that had already received wide-spread support, we now have a bill that represents a consensus reached among practically all groups and individuals, including those who spent an enormous amount of time and effort studying this question during the last few years. I am thinking more specifically, Madam Speaker, of Florian Sauvageau and Gerald Caplan.
This Bill increasingly represents a consensus, and if it is not passed and enacted very shortly, many Canadians, and I am thinking of ethnic and language minorities, Native people, the disabled and many other groups, would lose this opportunity to take their rightful place in an area that is very important to them the broadcasting sector.
Broadcasting Act

Before I conclude, I would like to note the contribution to this legislation of those in the Department of Communications, especially the Director General of Broadcasting and Cultural Industries, Christopher D. Burke, who passed away just a few days after this Bill was introduced in the House by his Minister.
On behalf of the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) and the Government of Canada, I would like to thank his wife, Debbie and son, Andrew who are in the gallery to mark this achievement, for Mr. Burke's outstanding service. In some important ways this Bill is his legacy.

Madam Speaker, I would like to remind all Members in this House who may intend to oppose the passage of this Bill that they will have to justify their actions before the Canadian public which is in favour of this legislation.
Finally, I believe we cannot afford to deprive Canadians of this modern and generous broadcasting policy we have before us today, and I am convinced, Madam Speaker, that what we know now will indeed be confirmed very shortly.

Madam Speaker, I consider the closing remarks of the Minister to be more or less a threat and really inappropriate at this particular moment, and I regret that those words have been said.
The occasion of this debate on final reading of this Broadcasting Act of Bill C-136, an Act respecting broadcasting and radiocommunications, is a very important one. This Broadcasting Act translated into legislative language is about Canada. It is about what Canadians will see and hear when they turn on their radios and push the television buttons on their TV sets. It is about how opinions are formed and how our society will respond, politically and socially, to our Canadian way of life over time. It is fundamental to Canadian sovereignty.
On the other hand, I had presented earlier, both in legislative committee and here in the House during report stage, on behalf of our Liberal Party, a substantial range of amendments which we believe necessary to make this Bill the legislative instrument required to meet Canada's TV and radio needs here and into the future. A number of amendments that we proposed have been accepted, and I appreciate the Minister's and the Government's openness in this regard. Nevertheless, the changes which have been accepted do not address some of the fundamental concerns we have raised throughout this debate, namely, that the cultural identity of our nation is to be preserved and strengthened.
I simply want to review the major policy areas where Bill C-136, as proposed, remains clearly inadequate. In choosing to focus on a limited number of key policy issues, however, I would not want anyone to think that Bill C-136 is otherwise acceptable. In fact, the Bill is seriously flawed, continues to be

September 27, 1988
Broadcasting Act
seriously flawed, and continues to reflect, as almost all witnesses who appeared before a legislative committee argued, the extreme haste with which this legislation has been rammed through the legislative process.
Major industry associations were forced to appear in midsummer before they had had proper opportunity to assess this very complex Bill, and to arrive at conclusions by their boards of directors concerning its implications.

Madam Speaker, Members who sat on the committee did not even have the opportunity to review the testimony and develop an enlightened opinion about the necessary amendments. The proceedings had precious little in common with the spirit of recent parliamentary reforms, especially the fact that the public hearings fell far short of the democratic process. The net result is a badly structured Bill which could not be properly amended to eliminate the obvious shortcomings.

I intend to indicate some of those very serious errors.
As concrete examples of this observation, I would like to indicate to this House and to the listening public that native peoples, aboriginal peoples, disabled peoples, and regional groups were not even heard when the legislative language translating the wishes of these task forces and standing committees were put before us. Multicultural groups got a hurried and last minute invitation to respond to extremely complex legislation.
Let me remind you, Madam Speaker, the concerns that we have about this Bill include many important matters, in addition to those that I wish to concentrate specifically on today. Among them are the following. First, that new concept of the definition of "program" in the Act. It is of serious concern, for it would split undertakings into two parts-a programming part and a non-programming part, creating a constitutional issue with the possible loss of federal jurisdiction over part of the undertaking. As well, their placement on the carriage priorities of our cable system is not clearly defined, and therefore could replace a channel even in the lower first 1 to 13 channel options that are available.
Second, the need to make provisions for broadcast programming in representative native languages is certainly not in this Bill.
When I hear the Minister's advocate talking about how this Bill is so vital and so important, it does not even bring in the major concern that the native constituencies brought to our attention in legislative hearings. They never were invited to present their view or an amendment during the legislative process related to the language of the Bill.
Third, the need to retain a seven-year term of office for the Chairman of the CRTC and the President of the CBC in order to protect the ability of both agencies to operate at arm's
length from the Government, just like that of the Bank of Canada, indicates the fundamental role and place of this essential service to Canadians and for Canadians. That has been overlooked and ignored. The potential for political interference is flagrant in this Bill. Much was improved, but this is one area that indicates a serious lack of concern on the part of the Government, or its desire to make some decisions with respect to how the whole system ought to operate beyond that which is totally acceptable.
Fourth, the need to define more clearly the roles of the CBC chairman and president in order to reduce the potential under the new Bill for conflict within the corporation. The question of who is the boss has been raised by many. We have had to live through some serious problems in Telefilm Canada because of lack of clarity and definition as to the roles of the chairman and the president. We are running into the same problem here. The Minister stubbornly did not wish to hear, nor did she appreciate, the very carefully thought through presentation made by the President of the CBC, Mr. Juneau who, knowing that he was leaving, left an excellent legacy for study and for an understanding of the role and the functions of chief executive officers and who has to make the final decision-where the ball stops.
Fifth, the Bill fails to provide priority for the carriage on cable of public sector broadcasting services, including those provided by both federal and provincial public broadcasters. It has not clearly defined cable priorities-carriage priorities to programming services and leaves all kinds of gaps and holes.
The most serious of those has been effectively spoken to by the listening public which is very angry about where the House of Commons channel appears, as an example, and I think with just right. In fact the pressure has been so much that Skyline has decided to move the House of Commons channel from out in space on channel 50 back down to channel 18. Approximately 70 per cent of Canadians have converters, so they can at least get channel 18, but perhaps it should even be down in the first 1 to 13 which is off air.
Apropos that, Madam Speaker, perhaps you take a look at what could be considered to be a definition of a public sector service. We talk about public elements and private elements. In the public element we would have our national broadcaster, the CBC, which the Government would like to define as the "mass audience appeal". Notwithstanding, there is the CBC, the provincial broadcasters, and also a new area where the Government has put in very significant funding. I am referring to TV 5.

The federal Government's $1.79 million contribution-18 per cent of the TV5 network budget and three times the amount put up by Quebec-and all the money invested by France make TV5 a public network which unfortunately does not reach beyond the borders of Quebec. This public network paid for by the public-you, me, all Canadian taxpayers- ought to be on the air from coast to coast in this country.
September 27, 1988



I have said from the first of our public hearings from the West Coast, through the prairie provinces, in Saskatchewan, in Alberta, and in Manitoba, that if we believe the fundamental characteristic of Canada is its bilingual nature, the public rule of law for the broadcasting system should include options and choices for both English and French from coast to coast. That stamp should be there. Certainly, if we are putting millions of dollars annually into a program such as TV 5, such as Radio Canada, such as CBC, there should be no options. That has been a standard undertaking on my part, expressed both in committee hearings across this land and in legislative hearings, and it has not been acted upon. It is a major hole in this Bill.
This shows a lack of application of the philosophy of official languages, of multiculturalism, of the whole concept of the fundamental characteristic of Canada, and it belies the reality of those laws.
The sixth point I would like to make is about the urgent requirement to avoid unfair competition and conflicts of interest by incorporating in law provisions limiting the role of cable TV systems to providing programming other than that which is complementary to that offered by licensed Canadian stations and networks. There has certainly been recognition that cable is a hybrid system. I have no objection to that. However, I have objection to unfair competition, and this would be unfair competition. I have been a strong proponent of available options and choices, but I think within reason and within the concepts of an economically viable broadcasting system for Canadians and by Canadians.
The Minister may say that is this is all very partisan, as she alluded to in her speech. Any one of us who objects to her point of view, just like any one who objects to the point of view of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), is not considered to have a valuable or valued point of view. It is not only me and this Party, but let me bring to Your Honour's attention what I would consider to be a rather informed, enlightened, and nonpartisan group that had something valuable to add to this whole process. I am talking about the Canadian Bar Association. I think it could be considered non-partisan. May I suggest that the Canadian Bar Association had some very constructive observations to make. It was able to appear before us on August 26.
I bring to the attention of the House and the general public that we only started hearings on August 10. We only advised the public that we would start these hearings in the middle of July. We now have before us some very valued advice. The following is what the Canadian Bar Association had to say: "The Media and Communications Law Section of the Canadian Bar Association brings together lawyers who practise in the communications field of law across Canada." I would say that is an enlightened group. It said: "This submission has been put together by a representative group of these lawyers based on their experiences in the broadcasting and communications law field. Given the importance of the new
Broadcasting Act
legislation, we are concerned that very little time has been given to interested groups to review the draft language of Bill C-136. In 1985 and 1986 many of the policy issues addressed in the Bill were given a full and comprehensive review as part of the work of the Caplan-Sauvageau task force on broadcast policy. In 1987 and 1988 many of these policy issues were reviewed again by the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture which commented on these issues in its fourth, fifth, sixth, and fifteenth reports."
They were rather extensive reports, and I can remember that the Minister's answers to a few of them were totally unacceptable. In one instance, I think it was two pages. It continued: "However, the actual draft language of Bill C-136 has been available for review by the public for barely two months. It is apparent from just a cursory review that Bill C-136 raises numerous legal questions which require interpretation and clarification. This is hardly surprising since the Bill represents the first thorough going revision of the Broadcasting Act in 20 years." I interrupt my citation to say en passant that it is true that it is 20 years. It did need review, but it needed time in its legislative language.
The Canadian Bar Association goes on to state that given the all-encompassing nature of the changes to the Act, however, and the likelihood that once enacted the new Broadcasting Act will be in place for a considerable period of time, it is essential in its view that Parliament provide a full opportunity for each clause to be carefully reviewed.
In making these comments, the interest of the Canadian Bar Association is not with policy issues as such. As noted above these have already been extensively debated. Rather its concern is with the legal language of the Bill.
In that connection it is particularly interested in ensuring that the Bill meets three tests: first, that the language should be clear, unambiguous, and readily understandable; second, that the Act should be sensitive to questions of fairness and due process in the administrative law context; third, that the Bill should be consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. In all these respects its review to date indicates that the wording of Bill C-136 gives rise to a number of concerns. Many of them are of a technical nature, but others have a more substantive character.
I really should read into the record the 29 pages of amendments that follow its comments but I will not. I will, however, bring to Your Honour's attention that 44 amendments were presented in committee and 12 at report stage, for a total of 56. That indicates how flawed the Bill was in the first place.
The association has indicated problems with the definition of broadcasting, the programming undertaking and distribution undertaking definitions and technical matters, definition of the term "public", applicability of regulations to exempted persons, responsibility for programs, overlaps in Section 5(2) and Section 3(1), and clarification of the word "element".

September 27, 1988
Broadcasting Act
These are all amendments I brought to the House and suggested we look at them in legislative committees. Certainly not all of them were considered favourably by the Government.
The second thing it looked at was CRTC powers and procedures. It has very serious concerns around who decides, the seriousness of the due process, and the increase in CRTC powers. The last area it deals with rather extensively is freedom of expression and charter concerns. Not only did the CBA have serious concerns, every single group that came before us did as well. There were at least 40 recommendations for amendments of substance and an additional 30 linguistic corrections, and that suggests there is much cause for concern.
With respect to the linguistic corrections I was quite fascinated with an observation they made. This should give us pause. They say that this is undoubtedly the first time in the legislative history of Canada that the French version of a statute has been longer than its English equivalent. While the emergence of a new style of legislative drafting is to be applauded, there is a general loss of accuracy and consistency, which leads to some serious problems in the equal application of the law across this land.
There is another point of equal importance that was not seriously addressed satisfactorily, and that is the light weight given to educational and community broadcasting, which have now been moved jointly into a subparagraph. This certainly does not reflect the attention given by either the task force or the standing committee recommendations in this regard.
I heard what the Minister said in her speech about educational broadcasters. I certainly recall what she had to say about memorandums of understanding and so on. I suggest that the effect of the proposed legislation on educational broadcasters and the people we serve cannot be underestimated. This is not just some piece of legislation. The Broadcasting Act covers one of the largest industries in Canada whose products touch the lives of every man, woman, and child in this country. What the Criminal Code is to the administration of justice, the Broadcasting Act is to the lives of these people.
We believe the new legislation sends the wrong signals. I recommended that we restore educational broadcasting to at least its former position in the 1968 Act where it is described as integral to the Canadian broadcasting system. With respect-
[ Translation]
... to community programming, Canada generally and Quebec especially have played a pioneer role in the world in the area of radio broadcasting. Such stations as CINQ and CBBL in Montreal are models in the area of community programming and have many copied emulators in Canada, especially in Quebec. It is therefore somewhat suprising to discover that a clear definition of community programming is
not found in this Bill. It is not a local project. Local programming is not a sufficient definition.
It might be considered as coming under clause 3.(l)(j)(ii) dealing with local broadcasting. But again, would it matter to determine what are the responsible parties? How will community programming be financed and by whom? Who would have access to it, so that such global policies as those mentioned in the Standing Committee report may be developed and implemented?

This was brought to our attention very forcefully by the ethnocultural communities, as the educational concern was brought to our attention by the spokespeople for the educational sector. I think there was something to learn from that but the Minister obviously did not hear.

We have a nationalistic Minister who cannot get those big ticket items through Cabinet. In my speech I will speak about those items in some detail. He says that the Canadian public is in favour of this Bill. Where? Show me where the Canadian public is in favour of it. I think that the Canadian public would be in favour of a nationalistic
________________________________19683
Broadcasting Act
Bill that would protect Canadian culture. Why not try the Canadian public on that? The Government has not done this.
Let me deal in more detail with what the Bill does and where the flaws are in the Bill. I said in my second reading speech on this Bill that the problem with Canadian broadcasting was that the public sector was under funded and that the private sector was not doing its job in producing Canadian programs. I do not think that this Bill is going to change that, fundamentally.
This Bill, when it came in, was worse than the 1968 Act. It has been amended. I would say that it is marginally better now, but that is not saying very much because the 1968 law is 20 years old. We had this great opportunity to put a really great Act in here, and I do not think that we have done that.
In the past 18 months, we have seen a government policy. Just look at what has happened in cultural policy. First, we have seen the reduction of the capital cost allowance for Canadian films and television programs, and that had encouraged production of Canadian films and television programs. That action is going to discourage it. We are going to have less production of Canadian films and television programs as a result of that government action.
We saw the revision of the film products importation Act, which now substitutes grants instead of structural changes. The Government had to retreat in the face of pressure from the Reagan administration. Jack Valenti got what he wanted on this. That retreat was a shame, a blot on the Canadian Government. We saw the Minister's old film Bill, and then we got the new Bill which was clearly a retreat, and we can document that.
Third, we got the rejection of the Investment Canada guidelines for film distribution proposed by the 1985 film industry task force, recommendations that would ensure the orderly transfer of ownership and film distribution to Canadians. They were ignored. We then got the failure to apply the 1985 Baie Comeau book publishing policy, which promised to see the transfer of ownership in book publishing to Canadians; in other words, to protect Canadians in takeovers and apply a tough rule so that we could have Canadian ownership of publishers.
Finally, we see in this Bill the rejection of key recommendations of the broadcasting committee. These proposed measures would have significantly enhanced the production of Canadian programs for a Canadian market and have a significant beneficial effect on the recording sector.

Association of Motion Picture and Electronic Recording Artists; Canadian Conference of the Arts; Canadian Film and Television Association; Canadian Independent Record Production Association; Canadian Periodical Publishers Association; Directors Guild of Canada; National Association of Broadcast Employees and Technicians; Periodical Writers Association of Canada; and The Writers Union of Canada, all raised these issues. They said this:
It seems clear that the Free Trade Agreement will alter not only the course of our economy, but by inhibiting our freedom to strengthen vulnerable yet essential cultural industries, it will also alter the course of how we define ourselves as Canadians. The Agreement recognizes a North American reality, but it leaves little room for a Canadian vision.
You have to see this Broadcast Act in that context, in the retreat of Canadian cultural policy initiatives, because of the free trade deal.
I had a number of motions to amend the Bill which I described as key amendments. I draw Your Honour's attention to Motions Nos. 36 and 39. In Motion No. 36 I suggested that we should put in the words "deliver only duly licensed services". In other words, we would have to license all programs coming into Canada. In Section 39,1 said:
"(ii) should ensure that foreign services, with the exception of conventional off-air broadcasters, are complementary to Canadian services."
I took recommendation 58 of the broadcasting committee of the House of Commons, an all-Party committee, and I really adapted that. Let me just quote that recommendation. In referring to the Broadcasting Act, it says:
The act should be drafted so as to define the essential role of distribution undertakings as that of distributing Canadian radio and television services in French and in English, both public and private, with first priority given to public-sector Canadian services, followed by private Canadian services. With the exception of the "three-plus-one" services already carried, the act should make provision for the carriage of foreign radio and television services only when the programming they provide is complementary to that available from licensed Canadian broadcasters and network operators.
The act should also provide for priority to be given to the carriage of services in French in distribution undertakings that serve primarily francophone subscribers.
What does that mean? It means that we have American superchannels that will now start coming into our country. They are Canadian channels. If a Canadian channel starts up, something like Arts and Entertainment, it will not be able to compete with the Americans. It will be knocked off the air. Our news channel, like CNN News, will be involved. We will get American news, American entertainment. There is nothing wrong with American news and American entertainment, providing we do not have the Canadian equivalent. What we and the committee are saying is that they can only come in if there is no Canadian equivalent. If there is a Canadian equivalent, keep them out. In other words, they have to be complementary to the Canadians. That is the key.
We would not interfere with NBC, ABC, CBS or the Public Broadcasting System of the United States. They are well established in the Canadian market. We also would not interfere with the border stations. These new channels, if they
come in, will swamp the private Canadian channels, that cannot compete with them. That is the key to this Bill and that is what the all-Party committee was recommending, but the Government did not act on it.
The Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) dealt with the reasons the Minister gave-I do not have to repeat them-why they could not license them and so on. She had legal argument and authorities to back that up. The Government backed off from this because of the free trade deal. It is a fundamental flaw in this Bill and one of the reasons we cannot support it.
I will just quote what the sixth report said:
We note that even in the large U.S. market, where service is provided entirely in English, there is only one available service in most programming categories. In Canada it is beyond question that a Canadian service could not co-exist with a non-Canadian service, especially if the Canadian service is expected to provide a meaningful contribution to Canadian programming.
The Canadian Broadcasting League said:
If this country had adopted such an approach 60 years ago this country would never have developed a separate Canadian broadcasting system except in the public sector.
That is the first fundamental flaw in the Bill. I believe we are approaching one o'clock, but perhaps I could get started now and deal with the second flaw in the bill, the use of cable systems. They are the big winners here. They seem to have a lot of influence in the Conservative Party these days. What a gift they got in this Bill! They got the right to import almost anything into Canada, that is, there are no express limitations on what they could take. This is part of continentalization.
Second, they got the right to originate programming, not just local community programming to which no one objects, but to originate all kinds of broadcasting programs. They are not treated as a distribution undertaking now but as a broadcasting undertaking. I predict that the result will be that we will not be able to regulate any more, or even in the future, their tariffs and their fees properly.
Canadians in the last few weeks have seen cable fees go up on September 1. This Bill gives a great gift to the cable companies in that it allows them to broadcast, and it will make it more difficult in the end for us to regulate their prices.
This afternoon I want to come back to the CBC and to the role of the public sector, and then to wrap up my speech.

subsubtopic: OLYMPIC GAMES-BEN JOHNSON, DISQUALIFIED 100 METRE WINNER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after an inspiring beginning, the Ben Johnson story appears to have had a brutal and disappointing end.
While drugs should not and cannot have any place in athletic competition, and while there can be no alternative but to bring the full weight of our own sporting regulations against Ben if he knowingly consumed the illegal substance, I was dismayed at the performance of our Canadian officials during last night's press conference in Seoul, Korea. They seemed to trip over each other in their rush to accept the guilty verdict, without attempting to defend the possible innocence of our own champion and Canadian citizen.
Given the tampering allegations, and the repeated denials of Ben and his coach, it would not have been too much to ask our officials not to render a guilty verdict until a thorough investigation was conducted into all the allegations and circumstances, and the roles of all the other people who were involved.
To accept the IOC ruling is one thing; not to defend the possible innocence and honour of one of our own, is quite another. If it had been Carl Lewis, one can rest assured that the Americans would have raised proper hell. I am puzzled and disappointed at why our Canadian officials were so anxious to drop Ben Johnson in front of the entire world.

subsubtopic: POSTING OF ELECTORS' LISTS-RISK POSED TO VULNERABLE PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as most Canadians are aware, we are very close to another general election. Yet there is a bit of a flaw in the process inasmuch as when the enumeration lists are posted, the names of all those people eligible to vote are available to the general public. Because of this exposure, senior citizens who live alone, and single women who live alone, become very vulnerable to those who would take advantage.
As we look to another election down the road it is very important that everything that can be done should be done to protect those people from becoming victims of people who would want to take advantage of them.

Mr. Speaker, recently the last remaining shipyard in the city of Vancouver closed down, and 150 more workers lost their jobs. For over 50 years shipbuilding had been a major west coast industry. The Conservative Government, through lack of any comprehensive shipbuilding policy, and inadequate subsidies, is directly responsible for the demise of this important industry.
The delay in building the promised world-class Polar 8 icebreaker has also contributed to this tragedy. In 1985 the Government approved this major project to be built jointly in Vancouver and in Victoria, but apparently promises are to remain on paper. Vancouver, which initiated the Polar 8 coalition, has been dealt out of the deal.
Thanks to Tory neglect, highly skilled tradespeople who should be building vessels for the longest coastline in the world, have been put out of work. Unemployment in Vancouver East remains at over 20 per cent.

OLYMPIC GAMES-BEN JOHNSON, DISQUALIFIED 100 METRE WINNER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I praised Ben Johnson's triumph at the Olympics, and noted that his example had inspired hundreds of young people at a rally in the Jane-Finch area of my riding. The rally was organized by a caring community under the title "Say No to Drugs".
The sad developments overnight are a tragedy for Ben and for Canada, but there is still a lesson there for young people whom Ben inspired. Saying no to drugs is worth it.

subsubtopic: PROTECTION OF ENVIRONMENT AND NATURAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to tell you about something ridiculous. A common front of ecologists is afraid that the Free Trade Agreement might undermine the powers of the Canadian and provincial Governments with respect to the environment. These people claim that the FTA would have a catastrophic impact on Canada's ecology and resources.
That, Mr. Speaker, is utterly false and tantamount to misleading the Canadian public. The Free Trade Agreement takes due account of the fact that, in January 1986, the Canadian Advisory Council on the Environment, widely known for its independent approach, set three conditions: our ability to manage our renewable and non-renewable resources, control pollution and waste disposal, and protect our ecology.
A concrete example would be the maple bush fertilization program which is being developed, Mr. Speaker. Besides, FTA Article 603 confirms the right of Canada and the United States to pass regulations aimed at protecting human, animal and vegetal life as well as the environment. That happens to be a sovereign attribute of each country. They should stop their scaring tactics.

Rod Murphy (Churchill): Mr. Speaker, since 1984 there has been a cease trading order against Gold Lake Mines Incorporated. This company owes many Manitobans thousands and thousands of dollars. It owes up to $75,000 to one retired couple in the Bissett area.
Unfortunately, through our federal and provincial laws we are unable to protect these people. I call upon the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) to check into this case, find out why this American-based firm is still operating through a different name in Manitoba, still filing mining claims in Manitoba, and is not being responsible to those people to whom it owes so many thousands of dollars.

CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-ENERGY INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last weekend on television the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) stated that Canada has sold out its energy in the Free Trade Agreement.
That is incorrect, and it is wrong. Nothing could be further from the truth.
We do not have to sell our energy to anyone. The control of all our resources remains in Canada. Each province has under its jurisdiction the right to control the exploration, development, and the sale of its oil and gas. Pricing is based on international prices, not U.S. prices.
We moved to deregulate the oil and gas industry in 1985. That removed that disastrous Liberal National Energy Program that robbed western Canada of billions of dollars. Our energy policy is now and will always be made in Canada, by Canadians, for Canadians. The Free Trade Agreement secures access to the U.S. market for our energy products and that will lead to future development and security of supply for all Canadians.

subtopic: OLYMPIC GAMES-BEN JOHNSON, DISQUALIFIED 100 METRE WINNER
OLYMPIC GAMES-BEN JOHNSON, DISQUALIFIED 100 METRE WINNER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport. I want to say at the outset that I agree with the Minister that it is a most difficult situation and my colleagues and I share with him and all other Canadians the regret for what has happened and the events which have unfolded in Seoul over the last 24 hours.
We have had the irrefutable evidence from the IOC, which none of us can challenge. On the other hand, we have the statements attributed to Ben Johnson and to his coach. We have seen quotes from his manager, from his family, and from people who trained with him, who suggested Ben would not have knowingly, and I emphasize the word "knowingly", taken steroids.
I want to ask the Minister in all seriousness what steps the Government of Canada is going to take to try to determine
September 27, 1988

exactly what has transpired and what led to Ben Johnson having steroids in his urine after the gold medal event?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of State (Youth)) and Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth)
subtopic: OLYMPIC GAMES-BEN JOHNSON, DISQUALIFIED 100 METRE WINNER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my understanding of the unfolding of the events is that the first test produced positive. 1 think the Hon. Member is very aware of the mechanics around the test. Following the first positive test, there is an opportunity offered to the athlete and the Olympic Association of the country to be heard and offer an explanation, which was done.
I think the Hon. Member refers to the explanation offered by the Canadian Olympic Association on behalf of Mr. Johnson, the possibility of an inducement of steroids after the race. My understanding of the results of the test, and that was in the press conference yesterday, is that what they call the imprint in the analysis was not compatible with that scenario.
The IOC decision is without appeal. We cannot affect that. That decision being rendered, it is now up to the IAAF to act. My understanding is that it will impose a suspension for a minimum of two years. Then it is left open to Mr. Johnson to appeal that. I understand that the due process of law will be respected. He will have an opportunity to be heard and to make his case and to explain whether, as the Member points out, perhaps knowingly or unknowingly, he used the steroids or not. We expect that will happen. I have that assurance, I think, from the President of the Canadian Track and Field Association with whom I spoke yesterday and whom I know well, and I am persuaded that that opportunity will be offered to Mr. Johnson.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is also addressed to the Minister. I have two points. Last night on CBC, Lyle Makosky, the Assistant Deputy Minister, indicated that the Government of Canada would be pursuing some form of investigation.
The Minister stated earlier today that in fact Mr. Johnson was tested in August in Zurich, and I assume found to have no trace of steroids in his system, and I am advised that it would be unlikely that in such a short period of time, from August to the day of the event in Seoul, there would be little if any benefit from the use of anabolic steroids for an athlete in such a condition as Ben Johnson. Will the Government undertake that investigation, an independent investigation, separate from anything that the sports governing bodies in Canada or internationally may do, so that Canadians, Ben's coach, and Ben himself can find out exactly what happened?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of State (Youth) and Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the conversation I had yesterday with the President of the Canadian Track and Field Association, we agreed that we
Oral Questions
would let the games finish and let time pass to let us all catch our breath and, as we say in French-
[Translation] let the dust settle.

-and that we would discuss with them the terms of an investigation to look at what happened, not only as far as the involvement of Ben Johnson is concerned but of those who are in contact with him, because it is a matter that needs to be cleared up. There are certainly a lot of questions left to be answered and we will want to do that, but I would like to stress that I would certainly prefer to enter into these actions in a context that is not the one we have today, and let a little time pass.
I may want to draw one distinction. We did ask for an inquiry in the area of weightlifting, but the circumstances were different from the ones of today. There were other circumstances that made us act immediately.

subtopic: OLYMPIC ATHLETE BANNED FROM NATIONAL TEAM
OLYMPIC ATHLETE BANNED FROM NATIONAL TEAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of all of the facts and the admitted breaches of security in the holding area for athletes at the Olympics following the race, which the highest officials have admitted took place, I would like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister a question.
September 27, 1988

Does the Government not feel that the Minister of Fitness and Amateur Sport was a trifle hasty, to say the least, in condemning Ben Johnson to a lifetime ban when Ben Johnson said he did not take steroids, when his family said he did not take steroids, when his coach said he did not take steroids, and when every test done in the past showed that Ben Johnson did not take steroids and this Minister did not even talk to Ben Johnson to get his side of the story?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of State (Youth) and Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth)
subtopic: OLYMPIC ATHLETE BANNED FROM NATIONAL TEAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am disappointed by the attitude of Members of the Liberal Party, and I fail to see what they are seeking to accomplish with this tactic. Suffice it to say that the rules are very clear and have been clear for some time now under this Government. An athlete caught in a doping situation is suspended for life from Sport Canada funding and cannot participate in a national team that receives funding from the national Government.
There is an appeal available to the athlete. He has a 30-day appeal period and he can use it, but I want to stress one thing. There is a reason why we are so severe. It is for the athletes. The drugs, the steroids, actually kill them, and we do not think that we should enable that to happen in our sports system.
Mr. Speaker, a man is innocent until proven guilty. No one is questioning the contents of the urine sample.
Oh, oh!
Why don't you tell Kaplan that?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The Hon. Member.

No one is questioning the contents of the urine sample. However, there was a general lack of security at the Olympics. Ben Johnson was there a week and a half prior to the race. Even the highest officials admit that there was a breach of security in the so-called accreditation area. There were a number of ways that Ben Johnson could have been framed.
I will direct my question to the Prime Minister. Because of the possibility that Ben Johnson could have been victimized, and because he is such a superb athlete who has passed every single drug test he has taken in the past, does the Prime Minister not feel that the Minister of Fitness and Amateur Sport should be reprimanded for repeating what he called rumours about Ben Johnson to the entire world without giving Ben Johnson a fair hearing? Or is the Government just putting on an air of righteous indignation in an effort to impress the world?

The rules that are laid out by the IOC are very clear. The opportunity of a hearing was offered to the Canadian Olympic Association, which took up the cause and made representations on behalf of Mr. Johnson and also made representations and explained what Mr. Francis said. subsubtopic: BRUNDTLAND REPORT-PRIME MINISTER'S SCHEDULED SPEECH TO UNITED NATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. He has given the Government of Canada's support to the Brundtland Commission and to its international report on the environment. My question concerns the Prime Minister's speech to the General Assembly of the United Nations on Thursday.
Does the Prime Minister plan to take some of the key recommendations of the Brundtland Report to the United Nations? Specifically, will he include in his speech the urging of all members of the United Nations to include, as part of their foreign policy development, a foreign policy for the environment?

subsubtopic: BRUNDTLAND REPORT-PRIME MINISTER'S SCHEDULED SPEECH TO UNITED NATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend for his question on such an important matter. The Brundtland Commission Report developed the concept of sustainable development and did so in a particularly impressive way. Canada has endorsed that concept through CIDA. In fact, the Minister of Finance is in Berlin today introducing new initiatives from the Government of Canada in regard to our foreign lending and investments in the future, all of which sustain the general thrust of the Brundtland Report.

September 27, 1988
Oral Questions
We are very supportive of what Prime Minister Brundtland's commission put together. I will, of course, be addressing that issue and others when I speak to the General Assembly, and I thank my hon. friend for his views.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased, as one Canadian, to hear that the Prime Minister does intend to take the important matter of the environment to the United Nations. Picking up on what he just said about one of the recommendations of the Brundtland Report being to obtain national commitment from all nations in the UN to the notion of sustainable development, will the Prime Minister now make a commitment that this will be a sustainable policy of the Canadian Government and be applicable to all our agencies and programs as they impact on the external world?
Specifically, will he make a change in the Export Development Corporation's policy in Canada which, at the present, does not consider environmental impact at all in reaching its decisions? Will he assure the House that in applying this principle of sustainable development the Government of Canada will show a leadership role and apply it to all our external relations?

Mr. Speaker, the leadership role to which my hon. friend refers and seeks for Canada is one that, if I may say, was acknowledged by Prime Minister Brundtland herself in Toronto when she referred to the Government of Canada as one of the leaders, not only in foreign aid but in the marriage of foreign aid and sustainable development. This is very much an initiative of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister responsible for external relations, both of whom I think have provided important leadership in this vital area of our international life.
With regard to whether members of the United Nations such as Canada can do more, either in terms of aid or in marrying that aid to the concept of sustainable development, my hon. friend is quite right. We have not done enough as an organization. We have not done enough as a Parliament in regard to either international assistance or the harmonizing of that assistance with the concept of sustainable development. This Government and this Parliament will, I hope, do more.

subtopic: CANADIAN FUNDING OF UNITED NATIONS PROGRAM
CANADIAN FUNDING OF UNITED NATIONS PROGRAM
speechtext:

If he does intend to address the sustainable development notion in his speech, will he show that leadership by saying that the Government of Canada will apply that notion to all of our agencies and programs as they impact on the external world, beginning, for example, with the Export Development Corporation which does not now act on that basis? Would he give us the assurance that the Government of Canada will in fact be practising what it preaches?
Second, since the Brundtland Report also noted that the fund that has been established by the UN to monitor environmental issues on a global basis is seriously underfunded, that it has only about a $30 million budget at this point and Canada only gives about $1 million, will the Prime Minister use the occasion to demonstrate once again some Canadian leadership by offering a significant Canadian increase in terms of our share in the funding of that important program?

subtopic: CANADIAN FUNDING OF UNITED NATIONS PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada is not only a very significant contributor to the United Nations, to the Commonwealth, to la Francopho-nie, and to the Third World in general, but I can remember when there was doubt in the minds of some nations as to whether they ought to contribute at all to the United Nations. They were in substantial arrears.
I instructed the Government of Canada to make sure that on the first of January, in advance of Canada's dues being exigible, the Ambassador be there to pay Canada's dues to ensure that the signal went out that Canada viewed the United Nations as a most valuable organization which deserved the support of all nations.

speechtext: The environment fund.

We have, in Canada, a modern and, I think, moderate foreign policy. I will be discussing that in particular. Most recent is the role of Canada in international peacekeeping. For example, Canada today supplies the largest number of members of a peacekeeping contingent which is bringing peace to Iran and Iraq where only months ago thousands of people were being killed.
This is a contribution that Canada has made in the past. It is the degree of continuity that my hon. friend would seek and encourage. These are the kinds of important issues that I will be discussing on behalf of all Members of the House at the United Nations.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the recently appointed Minister of State for Transport. First I want to tell her that all of Niagara rejoices with her in her appointment.

September 27, 1988

second registry whereby large ocean-going bulk vessels, carriers from Canada, would not have to register under flags of convenience to remain competitive but would be competitive with a Canadian crew?

subsubtopic: SITUATION IN SOUTH AFRICA-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. A week ago, I put my question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and it was whether the Prime Minister would keep the promise he made before the United Nations that Canada would break off all economic relations with South Africa if there was no improvement in the apartheid system. In his answer, the Secretary of State for External Affairs more or less paraphrased the same promise, without satisfying anyone. My question is simply this: Will the Prime Minister keep his word on September 29?

subsubtopic: SITUATION IN SOUTH AFRICA-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the policy I announced, supported by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, was valid and remains the policy of the Government of Canada. In fact, last night at Laval University, the Secretary of State for External Affairs said more about the matter, introducing some new details on behalf of the Government of Canada. As far as we are concerned,

September 27, 1988
Oral Questions
apartheid in South Africa remains the greatest moral problem in the world today, and Canada together with its allies in the Commonwealth, the Francophonie, and the Group of Seven, is working very hard to break the system. I think that as a country we have taken some very important action since then, unique in some cases! We have taken further action together with various organizations and groups of nations and we are prepared to do more. Any decision as to breaking off our relations with South Africa will be made by Cabinet, if we conclude it is useless to pursue our present policy. subtopic: SEVERANCE OF DIPLOMATIC RELATIONS-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
SEVERANCE OF DIPLOMATIC RELATIONS-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION

Mr. Speaker, circumlocution from the mouth of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the mouth of the Prime Minister seems to be the order of the day rather than the key moral question that the Prime Minister made a promise three years ago before the United Nations that, if there was no change in the situation with respect to apartheid, he would sever all economic and diplomatic relations with South Africa. If there is one thing that is clear and ought to be clear to the Prime Minister, it is that there has been no improvement. There has been a marked deterioration.

subtopic: SEVERANCE OF DIPLOMATIC RELATIONS-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am astonished that my hon. friend would refer to the tremendous work of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and his responses in this regard as circumlocution. speechtext: I am trying to answer my hon. friend, if he will allow me. I think there has been strong, unanimous support by all Parties on this issue, from all corners of the House of Commons. subsubtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND-INSHORE FISHERY-ASSISTANCE FOR PLANT WORKERS AND FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. More than a month ago I rose in the House on a number of occasions to make the Government aware of the disastrous nature of the
September 27, 1988

inshore fishery in certain regions of Newfoundland year. I asked the Government to provide immediate financial assistance to the fishermen who are affected.
