speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway.

Thank you very much. I thank the Parliamentary Secretary.
When I was speaking before, 1 wanted to say this. When I spoke on second reading of this Bill, I said that the problem in the Canadian broadcasting system was that the public sector was underfunded and that the private sector was not doing its job in providing quality Canadian programming. That was it in a nutshell.
This Bill was originally worse than the 1968 Bill. It has been amended. I think it is better now than the old Act, the 1968 Act, but only marginally better. I think that we can do much better after 20 years. This is the first Broadcasting Act in 20 years.
I said this morning that the Bill is flawed in numerous aspects. We have had amendments, and they have helped. We had a good legislative committee. I see the Chair here. We got some amendments.
Here are the flaws of the Bill. First, I believe that the Bill leads to a North Americanization-especially in television-of our broadcasting. The Government rejected two key NDP
Broadcasting Act
amendments that would in fact say that American superstations on television, if you like-new stations-could only come into Canada if they were complementary to Canadian stations. That is, if they added something. If Canadian stations, like an entertainment network or an all-news network, already existed, then the American stations could not come in. That would take some guts for the Government to do.
We are not talking about ABC, NBC, CBS, the American public network or the border stations. We are talking about these new superchannels that are going to run right over us and perhaps put our Canadian private broadcasters out of business because they cannot compete with them. That is one of the flaws in the Bill.
I asked this morning why the Government did not accept these amendments. The Minister has many good intentions, but the fact is that the Government is hemmed in by all the parameters of the Free Trade Agreement with the United States. It cannot interfere with American investment or American industries coming into Canada, including the cultural industries.
The second flaw in the Bill is that the cable industry is being treated too well in the Bill. It is going to get the right to originate programming, in opposition to all previous reports, including the sixth standing committee report, the standing committee on broadcasting, and many witnesses who came to the legislative committee.
The problem is that we will have a potential for a monopolistic situation. We will have a vertically integrated industry that will now be able to broadcast as well as transmit. That could present some real conflict problems, because they will transmit their own programs, or they will be tempted to do that, or they will be in a potential conflict, as many witnesses stated.
The other problem is that it makes it more difficult for a regulatory agency or a government policy that really wants to hold down the prices of the cable industry, that wants to control the prices, as we control and regulate the telephone industry. We should be doing that with cable. That amendment was rejected. I see that the Liberal Party rejected my amendment on that. Canadians have seen, in the last month, cable prices go way up and different stations not available with their converter.
The third flaw in this Bill is that the CBC is seriously underfunded. If the Government wants to promote Canadian programming, it cannot do it by underfunding the CBC.
I want to quote Jamie Portman, a distinguished writer in broadcasting for Southam's, who said in an article in The Spectator of Hamilton:
The government has ignored a recent call from an all-party Commons committee that it show its commitment to better Canadian programming by increasing its support of broadcasting with up to $250 million in fresh funding annually ... in real dollar terms, the CBC's budget has shrunk by more than $150 million since the Conservatives came to power.

September 27, 1988
Broadcasting Act
I outlined in my speech on second reading that the budget has consistently gone down. Not only that, in order to make up some of that money, the CBC's budget or money that is taken in on commercials has constantly gone up. So we have a pattern of almost like a privatization of the CBC. They are relying more and more on commercials. They are more and more like a regular network. That was not the original mandate of the CBC.
I specifically point out the plight of CBC Radio, which is being underfunded. There are difficulties in the regions. There has been a cut-back of 28 per cent in regional programming. Why? Because the CBC had to take money and put it into its central dramatic program to meet its aim of 95 per cent Canadian content in drama-a good aim.
The Government cannot have it both ways. We cannot say that this is a Bill that is strengthening Canadian broadcasting and at the same time be taking money away from the CBC, because it just cannot be done.

Madam Speaker, speaking of the CBC, we must add that the French services have suffered most from the Conservative attack on the CBC. The French services produce more programs with a smaller budget than their English colleagues. As a result, we see fewer and fewer French drama series. You know that, Madam Speaker, as a former CBC actress!
Quebec's creative people, as the Coalition pour la defense des services franqais de Radio-Canada notes, almost always have to stay in their studios and cannot present their viewers with varied settings. Competing with Dallas takes money and resources.
Again, there is the same problem with French television. Resources are needed to produce those programs.
The third flaw in the Bill is that the Minister has talked about an alternate network in the Bill. It has been created with a wide mandate but there is no money for it. Therefore, we do not know when it is going to come in. We say: "Where's the beef?" If it is to be created in the Bill, where is the beef and the funding for it?
The fourth flaw in the Bill is with respect to the private sector. Through amendments we managed to get the notion of predominantly Canadian expression to apply to all the broadcasters in the broadcasting area. However, that only takes us back to the status quo that we had in the 1968 Bill. That is not acceptable to the NDP, when one considers that report after report has stated that the private broadcasters are not doing their fair share to create quality Canadian programming.
What does the Government do? In this Bill it sets out a performance incentive. That received no support in the
committee hearings. It is a strange scheme. A broadcaster receives a penalty if so many hours of Canadian programming is not produced. Canadian programming is costly to create as opposed to buying an episode of Dallas or an episode of another American program. I predict that the broadcaster will pay the penalty or the fine because it is cheaper. I do not think that we will see any major change there.
Various groups interested in broadcasting appeared before the committee. They opposed this Bill, and in a sense then yielded in their opposition; not that they accepted the Bill, but they were not quite as vocal against it. I made the following analogy, which I think is a good one. When you are being beaten by a two-by-four and someone switches and hits you with a little stick, you say that it is better than being beaten by a two-by-four. That is what has happened here. These groups are being beaten by a little stick after the Bill was amended, and not by the old two-by-four of the original Bill.
I say to these groups not to be weak-kneed, stick to your principles and keep going. There is a national Canadian vision here that could be in broadcasting. There is an election coming. I say to some of those groups that there could be an NDP government, or a minority House in which there will be a balance of power in a centre-left Government. In that case, the trade deal will be ended, and there will be an industrial strategy for Canada. Part of that strategy will be a cultural strategy. There will be a surge in cultural initiatives. There will be encouragement and much greater subsidization of Canadian programming and Canadian distribution, which will mean work for Canadian artists. It will be a Government that will not be afraid to cut back the carriage of so much American programming, and that will take some political guts. I say to those groups not to lose hope, and do not be weak-kneed and think that we have to get this Bill through or we will get nothing else.
There was an action day in which groups in Canada talked about what could be done. They stated that the need for better and more Canadian programming is now stronger than ever. Canadians have invested considerable time, energy, and money in developing Canadian programming. It would be a tremendous loss if we were now to restrict our efforts. We need to forge ahead to continue to reverse the flood of foreign programming on our air waves and in our cinemas. What could be done?
We could fund the public sector sufficiently, and have a five-year commitment to the CBC in order that it could carry out this wide mandate that it is being given under the Bill. We could restore regional service. We could support CBC Radio and stop the cut-backs. We could get the CBC to do the allnews network, and not cave in to the Conservative lobbyists with Allarcom and the group in Alberta. That is what we could do for the public sector.
We could say to the private sector that we expect a minimum of 50 per cent Canadian content in prime time between 7 p.m. and 11 p.m., and if you do not produce it, you lose your
September 27, 1988

licence. We will give some aid in a sense of helping the private sector to produce it, but we expect some results from the funding that they receive.
On the distribution side we could ensure that Canadians only receive the American specialty services when they are complementary to Canadian channels, for example, CBS, ABC, NBC, the border stations, and public American television, but not the superstations on some of those other networks, if we have the same service in Canada. If we do not have the same service in Canada, that is fine. But that cannot be done with a free trade deal, and that is why the free trade deal must go. If there is a minority Government, or anything other than a majority Conservative Government, that trade deal is gone.
Finally, on the distribution side, we must make a clear division between content and carriage. The cable industry, like other monopolies, should be regulated for the good of the people, and its rate of return should be regulated.
We can do it. When I was growing up we used to say in English Canada, and perhaps it was not the same in French Canada, do we have a Canadian culture? Of course we have a Canadian culture. We have a French Canadian culture, we have an English Canadian culture, and we have a broader culture of the two groups above that. We, especially in English Canada, and especially on television, have to take those steps now to protect that, or we will lose it. We are being inundated.
As the Minister stated when this debate opened, Canadians watch 24 hours of television a week, and young people watch more. We have to make sure that Canadians get Canadian choices of good, quality programming. This Bill will not do that. That is why we in the NDP will vote against it. That is why, if we have a say in the next Government, expect a strong, nationalistic, cultural Bill that will be unique in Canada's history. It will not exactly be unique, it will go back to 1932 when a Government had the guts to create the CBC and to create a strong public will in broadcasting. We have done it before, and we can do it again.

Madam Speaker, the pattern of rushing Bills through Parliament this session continues with the debate on Bill C-136. It was introduced on June 23, debated for two days at second reading, and rushed through a legislative committee that met and heard witnesses for just over one week.
In August the Association of Canadian Film and Television Producers wrote to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) asking him to slow down the deliberations of the legislative committee. The letter urged the Prime Minister to direct the committee, then acting "with undue haste", to devote "full diligence and consideration" to the Bill. That did not happen. The Bill was rushed back to the House. At report stage most of the amendments that would have made the Bill better were rejected by the Government.
Broadcasting Act
It is difficult to understand exactly what has been happening in the community. Many of the groups that spoke vehemently against this Bill in committee have now withdrawn their opposition, although they still say that the amendments should be passed. In other words, what we are hearing from the cultural industries is that it is a badly flawed Bill, but it is probably not as bad as what we may get after the next election, if the Government is returned. Therefore, let us pass it. It is only half bad and we might get something that is wholly bad. This is very difficult to understand. Why should we be asked to pass a bad Bill?
The co-chairman of the radio and TV task force, Gerald Caplan, co-author of the Caplan-Sauvageau report, having criticized the Bill for 18 months, then said: "It is better than the one we will get if this one dies and if the Tories come back after the next election with a majority". That is a strange argument for passing a poor Bill.
Indeed, the Bill is not all bad because no Bill can be all bad, but it could have been greatly improved had the Government been prepared to take seriously the committee stage and seriously examine the thoughtful amendments proposed by the Opposition. Perhaps one of the few positive things about this Bill is that it confirms the airwaves as public property to be regulated in the national interest. As well, the public network is still designated as "the principal vehicle for cultural expression in Canada". Having said that, it is difficult to find anything else that is positive in the Bill.
Let me look at the background to the Bill before returning to some specific criticisms. On June 23, 1988, the Government tabled a new Broadcasting Act and a broadcasting policy intended to replace the 1968 Broadcasting Act which provided the framework for developments in broadcasting in Canada for the last 20 years. The industry had been lobbying for many years for the Government to replace an admittedly outmoded Act, but what has been received is a Bill that does not go nearly far enough. It fails to make programming in Canada predominantly Canadian.
This is important because watching television is the number one leisure activity for Canadians, particularly young Canadians who are forming their views of their own country, of the world, and of their place in the world by watching television. This is true to a large extent. On average Canadians spend more than 24 hours per week in front of their television sets. Children watch almost 1,000 hours of television, compared to the 800 hours they spend in school. Canadians are radio listeners, too. Some 95 per cent spend 18 hours a week listening to the radio. More than 50 per cent of Canadians say that broadcasting is their principal source of news and information. Yet despite this heavy reliance on programming in Canada, most of what Canadians hear and see is not Canadian. Other world views, primarily American, are reflected.

September 27, 1988
Broadcasting Act
We need more access to Canadian cultural products because 80 per cent of our publishing industry is in foreign hands, 95 per cent of films shown in Canada are foreign, and 71 per cent of all programs viewed by English-speaking Canadians on television are American.
I think we would all agree that just any Canadian content is not what is required. The present Broadcasting Act, established by the previous Liberal Government, reflected that the goal was not just programs being made in Canada, but that they be programs reflective of Canada. Granted that fulfilling that objective was easier in the past before the predominance of cable TV, it was interpreted to mean that over half the programming provided by each station or network should be Canadian. The technical interpretation of the predominantly Canadian provision is unclear and the CRTC has allowed a number of services to operate with more limited levels of Canadian programming, particularly specialized limited audience services in ethnic languages or on pay TV.
In response to that the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, in its fifteenth report, recommended that the definition of "predominantly Canadian" be clarified so that the meaning would be obvious, that most of the programming provided would be indeed Canadian, and that the CRTC be allowed to exempt from the requirement the specialized limited audience services I just mentioned. For those services the requirement is not practical.
Originally the Government rejected that recommendation, but after much criticism from many experts a watered down provision was included in the Bill as Clause 3(l)(e). The Government accepted the standing committee's first recommendation but not the second. The redrafting is so poor that it is unclear whether the intent is the programming provided by Canadian broadcasters should indeed be predominantly Canadian. This clause is so important that the Bill should not be passed unless it is amended. Otherwise, without a clear requirement for Canadian content, the CRTC will have no legislative basis on which to maintain any such requirement.
Prior to the introduction of this Bill the Canadian broadcasting policy was based on two fundamental goals. First, to maintain a separate broadcasting system rather than simply allowing American broadcasters to extend their reach into Canada. Second, to ensure that those broadcasters provide a reasonable amount of Canadian programming. A major criticism that many people have advanced is the failure of this Bill to address carriage regulations for cable. This was seen as an urgent and important issue by the standing committee and the Caplan-Savageau task force on broadcasting which reported two years ago. The standing committee concluded "the carriage regulations for cable are at least as important as the requirements for individual broadcasters in maintaining any reasonable balance between Canadian and foreign programming in the system". Both committees concluded that the Government should define for the CRTC which channels cable systems should carry. The Bill, however, is silent on this issue.
The Liberal Party moved an amendment to define the role of distribution undertakings as that of distributing Canadian radio and television services in French and English, both public and private, with first priority given to public sector Canadian services, followed by private Canadian services. This amendment was rejected by the Government. It was modified and presented again and rejected again.
In the new Act there are also some changes in the CBC's mandate. In the 1968 Act the CBC was to provide "a balanced service of information, enlightenment and entertainment". The new Act states that the CBC should provide a wide range of information and entertainment programming. Why does the Government object to the word "enlightenment" as part of the mandate of the CBC? This has not been explained. In terms of actual practicalities, there are those who suggest that this could mean the end of programs like The Nature of Things, CBC TV, which attract large audiences.
I want to talk also about the situation with respect to condominium owners and this Bill. Owners of condominiums which have an MATV system are concerned that under Bill C-136 they will be considered a distribution undertaking and subject to licensing by the Canadian Radio-Television Commission. Their concern centres around the wording of the definition of "distribution undertaking" in clause 2(1) which, when taken together with clause 4(3), would bring MATV systems under the Act to the extent they receive and redistribute broadcast signals. The Canadian Bar Association addressed this issue in its brief to the legislative committee studying Bill C-136. It stated:
There continues to be an omission in the Act, namely, the situation where an apartment or hotel distribution system, either using encrypted radio signals, or closed-circuit cable system, provides programs solely to the tenants of the apartment building or the guest rooms of a hotel. Constitutional issues aside, in that case, the new Act would not apply to the system because the signals would probably not be thought of as being intended for reception by the public.
Prior to Bill C-136, the situation was different, but the unease among condominium owners continues. The amendments which would have clarified the situation have been rejected. My Party believes that condominium owners have the right to know where they stand with respect to this issue. The amendment proposed by the Lion. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), and rejected by the Government, clearly provides that assurance while allowing the CRTC to place terms and conditions to ensure fairness to local licensed cable television systems.
I have one final comment I want to make. It concerns the provision in this Act that allows the Government to give policy directions to the CRTC. This is worrisome. There is a point where it is logical but the Bill really is too open-ended. It would allow the Cabinet sweeping powers that ought to be spelled out in the law. Lately we are seeing quite a lot of the kind of drafting which allows the Government to make any regulations it chooses. This is a bad practice. It is a practice
September 27, 1988

which has escalated with this Government. I may say that the assignment of all power to the executive is also the hallmark of the new free trade bill.
Most of the experts in the field, including members of the Task Force on Broadcasting, thought the Government should have some policy-making authority over the CRTC. However, the trouble is that this Bill as drafted would open the door to those powers being used in a Draconian sense. Whenever we look at legislation, I suppose we always have to look at it with two optics. First, one can assume the legislation is going to be administered by sensible people and people of goodwill. Therefore, if one takes that position, one does not become too worried about having things left wide open to be subject to regulation. However, I think as legislators we cannot assume that every Bill will always be administered by people of goodwill and good sense. We do have an obligation to have some things clearly specified. I would suggest that the issue of the Government giving policy directives to CRTC is one which should have been specified very much more clearly rather than left to be regulated.
The Standing Committee also wanted some real limits set on foreign, mostly U.S., broadcasting services in Canada. The Government rejects this. Again, one can look at it from both points of view. We would all say that Canadians should have as much choice and freedom in choosing what to watch as possible. But the Government also has an obligation to encourage the development of Canadian talent, Canadian expression, and while there is a balancing act here, it would appear as though the Government is choosing to go the route of continuing to let our airwaves be swamped with American content, often American content which is not of any great artistic value.
This is a Bill which is a start but which needs a great deal more work. It is regrettable that the Government has not been prepared to look seriously at amendments or to do the necessary work to give us a Bill of which we could be proud.

Madam Speaker, I want to thank my hon. colleague for a very well presented argument in the interests of a Canadian content of the Canadian system. Because she sits on the committee on Finance and Economic Affairs and because she was well aware of the changes that were to be brought through tax measures, I would like to ask her about the capital cost allowance and the kind of exchange, perhaps, or the kind of concerns that that brought to her attention. I heard the Member say it was important to find the mechanisms to develop the artistic skills and demonstrate the competence of our own Canadian talent and to develop the opportunity to see the expression of Canadian talent on our screens. As the Member pointed out, American programs are very costly to produce. We need all the kinds of internal funding here in Canada that is possible.
The Minister has enriched the Telefilm fund, that is true, that is public money, but added to that we had the potential, through the Capital Cost Allowance, of increasing the
Broadcasting Act
incentives of the private sectors in the film industry. We were able, through this House, to persuade the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to reinstate the capital cost allowance for the mining industry but we were not able to do so for the film industry. I wonder if the Hon. Member would comment on that particular aspect which is in her portfolio.

Madam Speaker, I agree with the Hon. Member that one of the traditional roles of the CBC has been to showcase Canadian talent. We have all heard many briefs from those who saw the role of CBC as hopefully expanding in the future to showcase more Canadian films. There is indeed a very direct connection between the Member's question and this Broadcasting Bill before us.
I suppose the Government, in removing the tax incentives for the film industry, has taken the Draconian approach it has taken in a number of other matters. Granted, there were some lawyers, doctors and others who were doing very well financially out of sinking money into the film industry, and there was a place to close that loophole. To close a loophole is one thing but to close off an important incentive to creativity is quite another. Indeed, the Government went too far with its sledge-hammer approach.

Madam Speaker, it gives me some pleasure to be able to make a few further remarks on Bill C-136. I want to say how much I regret that the Government chose to defeat the amendment I put forward to this Bill as it affected the provisions for condominiums. Unfortunately, as a result of that, the anxiety of those people who happen to live in condominiums has not been satisfied at all, and their concerns will continue.
1 want to say a few words at the outset on the provisions of this Bill as it affects the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The provisions of the Bill dealing with the CBC, Canada's national broadcasting service, were greatly improved in the legislative committee. The Minister has acknowledged that the CBC is the principle vehicle for cultural expression in Canada, and in the committee, the committee members worked hard to ensure that the word "enlightenment" was returned to the mandate of the CBC. The regional programming provisions of the CBC's mandate which had been weakened in the Minister's original Bill were strengthened in committee and there were other important amendments made which have also added to the legislation.
However, the bottom line question is: "Where's the beef?" There is no use for the CBC to have a broad mandate if the network does not have the resources to fulfil it. Obviously, the specific question of funding is not a legislative matter. However, it remains fundamental that, on the question of funding and other non-legislative matters, we in the NDP have a profoundly different view from that of the Conservatives.
The fact is that the Conservatives have launched a vigorous and systematic assault on the CBC since they arrived in office

September 27, 1988
Broadcasting Act
in 1984. They took over from the Liberals who, in their last years in office, sought to solve the deficit problems on the backs of this country's cultural industries.
The CBC's parliamentary allocation has been cut enormously in real terms since 1984. In fiscal year 1984-85, it was cut by $905 million. The effect of the Government's policy, first and foremost, has been what could be called the de facto privatization of the network. More and more, the CBC has been forced to count on its own resources to stay afloat. Over the past four years, the evolution of CBC-generated revenue has also not been of great help to the CBC.
The pattern is clear. It has been to cut the CBC's public funding and to force it to increase commercial revenues and act more like a private station. As the CBC noted in its brief to the committee:
-this affects the quality and distinctiveness of the program schedule and it also means that creative risks have to be minimized or eliminated. This is not compatible with a Public Service mandate.
The damage has been most pronounced in the areas of regional programming. The standing committee set out in detail the crisis in the CBC's regional centres. In recent years, the network has been forced to cut 28 per cent of resources for regional programming in order to maintain network programming services on a national level. This has meant lost jobs and services for Vancouver, Calgary, Quebec City, Halifax and Chicoutimi, for example.
We have witnessed the forced centralization and privatization of the network itself. Peter Cochrane, a member of ACTRA, said the following in detailing the effects of the CBC cut-backs on the regions and on the quality of programming in general:
We think the emphasis that should be placed on local and regional programming must be large. Right now, with the reduction in budgets-and I am talking as I said, predominantly about radio-what has happened is that one of the finest radio systems in the world-and I think it is not arguable- has been eviscerated.
The general standard of programming, the general standard of what is made available to Canadians for the nurturing of their minds and their spirits, has become less and less and less effective. The stuff that is being reached out now and is being pumped into radios across the country is made level-a lot of it- generic pap, level pap, to which people are not required to respond.
We must remember that for the national broadcasting service to truly reflect Canada, there must be quality programming coming from all regions of the country and artists must have a variety of points of entry into the system.
The Minister has spoken of the money she has offered to the CBC in her new broadcasting policy in order for the corporation to reach the commendable aim of having 95 per cent Canadian content. In fact, the Minister is giving $20 million to the English service and only $15 million to the French service. This is great, but it does not come close to correcting the damage caused by the sledge-hammer cuts over the last four years. Even with the money, the CBC will not be able to meet the 95 per cent level unless it reallocates money, presumably from the regions, to meet this limited goal.
Thus, when we look at the substance and not the rhetoric being offered by the Minister, we find it lacking. The basic conclusion of the Caplan-Sauvageau report was that the CBC was the heart of the broadcasting system and it was seriously underfunded. It was the Conservative chairman of the communications committee who said that $250 million in new funding was needed to meet the country's broadcasting goals. This Minister has not even come close, as Dale Goldhawk, the President of ACTRA said, in responding to the Government's policy statement:
And while the CBC is expected to fulfill a wide mandate, the money to go forward simply isn't there. In short, this part of the announcement doesn't exactly make my socks roll up and down.
Pretty witty guy, he is. Gord Hunter of NABET has said the following on the Government's broadcasting policy:
The CBC has faced financial difficulty since the mid-1970s but the real assault began in 1984 when the Conservative Government took office. Each year the situation has worsened. I cannot see how the corporation could possibly be expected to increase its Canadian-content levels to 95 per cent when the funds allocated to it will not come close to paying for the service it was able to provide Canadians back in 1984.
In 1984 there was a very large budget cut at the CBC, and 1,200 jobs were lost. This reduction in funding and the subsequent reduction in staff has seriously reduced the CBC's capacity to produce and we have seen an ever-increasing reliance on advertising revenues to survive.
Two final points have to be made about the effects of the Tory cuts to the CBC and why the centrepiece of any broadcasting policy must be the restoration of CBC funding to the point that the network can adequately fulfil its mandate.
The first point is that the French services of the CBC, which produce more programs on a lesser budget, have been particularly ravaged by the Government's attack. The effect of this has been that the French network can rarely afford to produce teleromans and other programming which can have high production costs. Television series on Radio Canada can rarely go on location. Creators have stuck with simple in-studio sets with which they must compete with dubbed versions of Dallas and the like and we are committed to ensuring that the both the French and English services receive adequate funding.
Second, in the Minister's policy statement the Minister pays lip service to CBC Radio and its extraordinary success with Canadians. On a literal shoe-string these radio networks have produced an extraordinary array of fine radio programming. Every year we see it building an audience despite cut-backs that have led to more and more repeats. While the Minister throws crumbs to CBC Television, she does absolutely nothing for the suffering radio service.
I note that in the recent CRTC decision, which renewed the radio licences for only three years instead of five, the Commission said the following:
The overwhelming majority of interveners expressed strong support of CBC radio, stressing their desire to see the quality of service maintained and supported by adequate Government funding . .. Many interveners however,
September 27, 1988

expressed concern about the CBC's ability to sustain the quality of its radio services in the face of reduced federal funding.
1 do not want to take too long in this debate, but it seems to me that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is one of those structures in Canada that holds this country together much in the same fashion as a transportation system does. If the CBC were not there, many communities in Canada would not receive that kind of communication, very often because the private corporations and the private companies do not see a profit in providing that service. Canadians have recognized over the years that the only way that service can be provided is through a publicly funded corporation such as the CBC.
What we have seen over the last number of years is not so much whether or not Canadians deserve that type of service, but really an ideological approach to how Canadians receive these vital and necessary services. I want to say very clearly and very bluntly, not only to the Minister but to the Canadian public, that about the only Party which has consistently supported the kind of service provided by the CBC over the years has been this Party and the New Democratic caucus.
In conclusion, we in this Party and Canadians in general very much appreciate the tremendous amount of hard work that has been put into committee stage and all the proceedings that have gone on around this Bill by my colleague, the critic in this area, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). I sat in on several of the meetings when witnesses appeared before that committee and I was quite impressed at the way the Hon. Member handled himself and pressed forward our Party's position on this very important matter.

Madam Speaker, I would like to take advantage of the remarks which the Member has just made with respect to the work of his colleague. I would agree that it has been an extraordinary catch-up and he has done an outstanding job. I would also like to pay tribute, and I am sure he would agree with me, to the Member for Broadview- Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) who, unfortunately, cannot be here. She put about two years of her time and effort into the considerations as we travelled across this country with an excellent team of professionals and professional staff to come up with this report of our standing committee, which I think stands as a landmark view and review of the broadcasting industry.
I think we should pay our respects and particular accolades to the Chairman of the committee and the members of the committee whose names are quite well known at this point. Behind the scenes we had an outstanding Director of Research, Paul Audley; an Assistant Director of Research, Rene Lemieux; researchers from the Library of Parliament, Tony Jackson, Millie Morton, and James Robertson; and a Senior Consultant, Tim Creery. We had other consultants who I think deserve to be recognized. They include Peter Grant,
Broadcasting Act
John McKay, Jean Paquin, Robert Pilon, Mark Stiles, and Robert Storey. We had some outstanding editors and administrative assistants, secretaries, and assistants from Centralized Support and Translation Bureau.
I say this because I think it is important to acknowledge the role that was played by our staffs, both the staff to the parliamentary committee for over two and a half years and our own personal staffs behind the scenes who enable us to be effective in this House. Members are only as effective as the collegiality of the research body that helps us draw up these kinds of reports.
That being said, the Minister, who had her speech delivered by another Minister in the House early this morning, said that she felt that this Bill should go through, had to go through, that there would be very unhappy constituents out there if the Bill did not go through.
Does the Member believe that the broadcasting system of Canada would be more damaged with the new Bill than it presently is? Because the friends of public broadcasting, or because one of the authors of the task force report, Mr. Gerald Caplan, and perhaps because the NDP of Quebec region did not feel rather strongly that this Bill should go through, should we capitulate or have we, with the help we have had, done the kind of study that indicates that this is not a good Canadian Bill for Canadian broadcasting and for Canadian people?

I want to thank the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) for reminding me of the tremendous work that research and support staff do for Members of the House of Commons on our committee work. I agree with her that very often we do not pay as much attention or give as much praise, if you will, to those people who work so hard to make us look good very often.
In response to the Member's question, I heard my colleague, the Member for Vancouver-Kingsway, set out at least six points on which he expressed his concern over the flaws in the Bill. He has also indicated that we think that the Bill, with perhaps a little more consideration from the Government, would have been much stronger for Canadian broadcasting.
Having said that, I also appreciate the problem that the Minister has because of the debate that has gone on around the CBC over the last number of years. I can only guess at her difficulties in not accepting our suggestions. My friend, the Member for Vancouver-Kingsway, has clearly indicated that we do not feel that we can support the Bill in its present form. We very much regret that because we all would have wanted to make this review, the first real review of Canadian broadcasting in a number of years, a very positive one. Unfortunately, because of the flaws in the Bill, we do not think we will be able to support it.

speechtext: At this time it is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 66, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: The Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Oostrom)-Refugees-Case of Francesco Piperno sentenced for terrorism by Italian court; the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway)-External Affairs-Estonia-Recognition of Honorary Consul General.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Miss MacDonald that Bill C-136, an Act respecting broadcasting and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereto and in relation to radiocommunication, be read the third time and passed, and the amendment of Mrs. Finestone (p. 19682).

Madam Speaker, one of the casualities of this somewhat bizarre period we are going through, where the election campaign is being fought within the confines of Parliament Hill, rather than on the streets and hustings of Canada where it probably belongs, is that we are now being faced with exorbitant demands by the Government to rush through very important pieces of legislation that reach into the very vitals of this country in a very profound way without the proper examination, judgment, or reflection that such a policies require and demand.
In saying that, I want to pay tribute to my colleague, the Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), who against incredible odds has made every effort to introduce changes and amendments to the legislation that would reflect the testimony heard in the committee and draw out the concerns that so many organizations and so many Canadians have expressed.
The Bill was introduced only in late summer and Canadians have not been given the proper opportunity to engage in the debate that is required, especially when so much is at stake.
We are well aware that that some very important pressures are impinging upon the question of culture in this country. One is the explosion of a broadcasting technology that has exponential growth with the innovation and expansion of new forms of broadcasting and distribution in all varieties of communication. It simply astounds the imagination. One only needs to read recent articles that suggest the video recorder is on its way out. I went to buy a compact disc, only to discover that the salesperson told me it would be obsolete within months and a new type of tape would replace it.
Similarly in the area of broadcasting and the emergence of world-wide satellite technology and other innovations, it is absolutely imperative that we acquire a framework of public policy that is flexible enough to incorporate that change and still incorporate very specific values about what we as Canadians want to capture as part of the broadcasting spectrum so that Canadians would have a fair choice. That is one set of pressures.
The other set of pressures are applied as a result of our geographic location. It has been the touchstone of Canadian cultural policy since time immemorial. We have a neighbourhood relationship with a very powerful country that has been very successful in developing a dominating global communications empire. It is one of those areas of American industry that has dominated the world and which has developed an enormous political power within in order to protect itself.
I returned from the United States last week where I gave a series of lectures. It is fascinating to see how their view of their communication industry is, first, so different from ours, and second, so much dominated by a mixture of commercial and political forces to give it such incredible power within that country. Unfortunately, over the years that power has been exercised upon our country.
Canada is not seen as a distinct entity by the American communications industry, but simply seen as a suburb of Akron, Ohio, or some other regional variation to be addressed. There is no comprehension whatsoever on the part of that industry that it is dealing with a separate entity which has its own concerns, interests and values. We are simply treated as an appendage of its own distribution network. As a result, various Canadian governments over the years, Conservative and Liberal, have had to find ways to combat that while attempting to maintain an open communications system which offers a fair amount of choice without imposing complete isolation within national boundaries. It has been one of the most difficult balancing acts attempted by Canadian governments over time.
The Broadcasting Act has been an essential element in that policy. The American influence is not concerned about the Canadian Opera Company or the Royal Winnipeg Ballet. It is primarily concerned about popular culture, where it makes money. That is the American preoccupation. They would be quite willing to allow us to subsidize the Royal Winnipeg Ballet, but when it comes to popular culture in television, radio, film and publishing, it is a very different story and attitude.
This has been compounded very dramatically by a Bill that was also passed by the House just a few weeks ago. Bill C-130, dealing with the trade agreement, opens a whole new set of pressures and makes us even more vulnerable than we were to those commercial judgments.
Every cultural organization that appeared before the committee on Bill C-130, and others, pointed out that Article 2005 of the Agreement, the notwithstanding clause, gives the
September 27, 1988

Americans the power to retaliate on what they consider to be any future act of a Canadian government that will impinge upon their commercial interests. That is a Damocles sword over the head of Canadians when they try to deal with the expansion of new technologies and distribution networks. That will require major redefining, but Canadians will be faced with a sanction that will always be present if the agreement is ratified. Of course, that is something that we and a majority of Canadians hope will never come about. It is something still to be decided.
The debate on the Broadcasting Act must be seen in the context of that new development. It is not only a theoretical threat, it is one that has already been exercised. We have already seen the pressure applied with the kind of Valenti muscle that was exercised with respect to the radical alteration of the proposed film Bill the Minister talked about a few years ago. It has now become a pale ghostly shadow of its original self.
We have seen how that kind of American muscle has been applied in the publishing industry. The brave words of the former Minister of Communications about ensuring that takeovers and acquisitions would be carefully guarded have simply disappeared before the blind eye that has been turned toward this area.
Therefore we must question whether the Broadcasting Act will give us the ability to meet such challenges. Will it provide the ability and resources in Canada to meet the new technology and the very omnipresent and growing American demand for full and complete access and control of our popular communications systems? As has been expressed at second reading, at committee stage and during third reading by my colleague, this Bill has failed that fundamental test. It has not given any confidence that it will provide a strengthened defence in terms of retaining the capacity of Canadians to protect their popular culture systems and feel free that they will at least have an effective choice.
Part of that weakened defence has been the kind of undermining and erosion that has taken place on the CBC itself since the inception of the Government. We have seen the cutback on budgets and the informal but very clear intimidation on the public network. The limitation on its independent role severely weakens the network.
If the CBC is expected to carry the load in terms of dealing with the challenges I have outlined, then it has not been given the resources to do it. The tasks may be clear and identified but the flesh is weak. It simply does not have the necessary support and resources. The move to diffuse the role of the CBC into new channels and alternate networks without any accompanying infusion of proper resources simply dilutes its ability to meet its task.
I think that Members of Parliament should take seriously the kind of statements that were made by the President of the
Broadcasting Act
CBC in front of the committee about just how precarious a position it has been put in, just how difficult it is. It is unfortunate that that kind of ammunition was not recognized by way of changes to the Broadcasting Act, or further commitments by the Government. God knows it is not for lack of money. The Government has committed in the last three months $15 billion or $16 billion to various projects around the country. Obviously, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has found a new money tree somewhere, or the whole fiscal framework has been thrown out the window for the sake of the election. Within that $15 billion or $16 billion of new commitment, surely there might have been something more for the Canadian broadcasting network, in a substantial way.
If that is the number one requirement we have, why is it less deserving than a gas pipeline to Vancouver Island which in itself may be of some value? I am not here to judge that in this debate. But surely on the scale of priorities-and particularly the priority of what this national Government is responsible for-nothing is more precious or valuable than the communi-cation/cultural system of the country in light of the globalization and the Americanization that is taking place as part of it. Yet not one cent was provided to it.
Similarly, I want to point to the changed definitions that we apply to private broadcasters. It has been acknowledged that this is an area that has never been managed successfully. I do not think that anyone has been able to find the will or the fortitude by which to make a requirement for our private broadcasters to live up to a high level of responsibility. This is not a partisan attack. 1 include Governments of which I was a Member and which 1 supported over the last 15 or 20 years. I do not think we have ever applied the will necessary even through the CRTC or the Cabinet to make it stick. The price of a licence, being able to get on that airwave, I think, is an extraordinarily valuable entitlement, a rare one, a privileged one that we have given. Yet we have never asked for a full set of obligations in return.
There have been very powerful lobbies and very strong arguments, but the fact of the matter is that the private broadcasting system in this country has not lived up to its obligations to give Canadians real choices. You know the figures as well as I do, Madam Speaker, you have heard them in the Elouse. Some 98 per cent of our drama is foreign, most of it American. That is shameful.
If we look at the area in which we are supposed to have real competence, in news broadcasting and public affairs, something we have taken some pride in as Canadians, by comparison so little of the budgets of private broadcasters is spent in those areas-very, very little little of it. There is nothing in this Broadcasting Act which strengthens that. The very strong message that came out of the Caplan-Sauvageau report has somehow been dissipated, kind of vapourized in this Bill. In fact, I would have to say that the management of the present system gives signals of that kind, both at the level of the commission and at the level of the Department.

September 27, 1988
Broadcasting Act
I would like to give you one example, Madam Speaker. I have now received I do not know how many inquiries or demands from my own constituents about the displacement of the parliamentary channel from the cable system on to a cable system that requires a new converter. In my riding there are a lot of people who can neither afford a new converter nor a new TV set. They simply do not have the money. Yet they have found a great satisfaction-sometimes one wonders why-in watching the parliamentary channel, watching Question Period and debates. A lot of people feel that that is a very important exercise of their citizenship. As a Member of Parliament you yourself, Madam Speaker, would know how people draw to your attention when you have been saying something good, bad or whatever. That has become, in part, an ingredient in our culture over time. I guess we can say that it is certainly no worse than the soap operas with which it competes. Certainly, we have all learned how to dress more appropriately at least.
Why would we allow a system, a judgment that brings MuchMusic on to the cable systems, which is okay? I watch it. It is kind of fun at times. Or why would we allow a system that brings a new family channel or a new religious channel, both of which are valuable and have a minority interest but which displace the opportunity for Canadians to watch their own Government in action?
I have written to the Chairman of the CRTC about it. We have raised the matter in the Elouse. The fact of the matter is that it says something. There is a signal out there that no one is minding the store. No one is applying themselves to that kind of judgment. It slipped by and everybody is backing off. It is like watching those sports officials in Seoul last night who were saying: "It is not my fault". Talk about passing the buck. I am afraid that that has become too much of a pastime under this present regime. Yet here is something that is very crucial to Canadians and we have allowed it to take place.
Let me give you another example, Madam Speaker. [Translation]
I think it is very important for all Francophones in Canada and in fact the whole country to have access to Channel TV5. Especially since the Government of Canada paid most of the money for this service. There is a service for Quebec and for the "Francophonie" but not for Ontario and certainly not for the West or the Atlantic provinces.
I think the people of my riding have the right to have access to Channel TV5. But the Government of Canada isn't there to make a clear-cut decision that will get the service for the entire country.
Madam Speaker, this is one more example of the lack of direction in Canadian policy. It's fine for Senegal to receive Canadian programs, but I think people in Winnipeg, Saskatoon and Moncton should enjoy the same privilege. This is one more example of the vacuum that exists in our communications policy.

That is the problem. The Broadcasting Act is not a piece of legislation that reflects a coherent set of judgments about what Canadian communication policy must be in light of the kind of conditions. It has been kind of patched together to satisfy one interest over another. A little cloth has been cut here and something has been tailored there, but it does not represent the kind of framework of broadcasting that the future of this country will require, especially in light of what we face.
I see you are asking me to conclude, Madam Speaker. I would like to cite one small example which will just take a moment. I refer to the amendments proposed at committee concerning the question of satellites for condominium owners. The amendments which we had gave proper credibility to the right to license programming coming in, but they also gave the technology access. The amendments proposed would have created a system equal to all Canadians. But it was also rejected even though it was supported by all sides of the House-by New Democrats, Tories and Liberals. Once again, there was a kind of blankness and refusal to respond to those kinds of conditions, simply because it was already fixed in stone.
The great regret of this-and it may be a product of haste and rush-is that it is not the kind of Broadcasting Act that Canadians either need or deserve, and it will not provide the kind of important front line argument and structure that we will need to deal with the future, especially as it relates to the preservation of Canadian culture.

Madam Speaker, I want to say to my hon. colleague from Winnipeg-Fort Garry that I was very pleased to see him mention, first of all, TV5, as it would bring a cultural perspective of French Canada to all Canadians. Many Canadians are bilingual, and I am sure that they would be interested in watching it. It would also bring in the international aspect of France and Belgium and Senegal.
It would seem to me that when we are spending Canadian public-federal dollars there is no reason why that public-federal service should not be available, if we truly believe that the fundamental characteristic of Canada is its bilingual nature. I can remember the arguments around the French and English on the cornflakes box. I hope we are not going to go back to that silly business.
You, I know, have had an ongoing interest around condominiums, and I was glad to hear you mention that. But because you mentioned at the outset of your remarks that you have been in the United States recently-

speechtext:
I would appreciate it if the Hon. Member, even in the period of question and comments, would come through the Chair to ask her questions and address the Hon. Member. It was done before and I let it go. The Hon. Member.
September 27, 1988

Thank you very much, Madam Speaker. You are right. I had forgotten the protocol of the Chair. Through the Chair, I would ask the Hon. Member if in his recent trip to the United States, and with his knowledge of the free trade Bill, he would see that although the Minister may well have wanted to have had a Canadian Bill that would reflect Canadian concerns, because the entertainment aspect is not seen as a cultural aspect in the United States, that had some true implication for the potential for licensing any and all satellite-to-cable programs, direct-to-home, which perhaps can soon be part of the new technology, or the direct broadcasting system, the concerns that new technologies will bring, and if we do not control them, we are going to have an even greater problem on our hands.
What would his view be regarding entertainment versus cultural programs, or cultural sovereignty?

In response to my colleague from Mount Royal, it may be that too few Canadians and perhaps too few Members of this House have taken the time to read carefully both the American implementing legislation dealing with the trade agreement and, perhaps more important the accompanying document that was issued by the President called Administrative Action. Within that document you will find that the Americans make very specific definition as to what they consider to be the impact of the trade agreement. They believe that any attempt by Canada to subsidize a cultural or communication activity that will injure their commercial interest will now be subject to a substantial countervail retaliation, not just in the area of culture but in other industries as well. They can attack hydro or automobiles for undertaking that kind of action.
It is interesting to note, in exchanging views with American experts in the field, which I have done in various meetings over the past week, that their view is that that is one of the great advantages that they have won as a result of the trade agreement. They have been able to see this as a way of substantially restricting any further attempts of Canadian content rules or limiting distribution in other areas. That is part of their win-win proposition.
The definition, of course, is one that is very clear. They see it purely as an enterprise. Perhaps you have to understand that is a country where there is virtually no foreign broadcasting. I guess the odd British film shows up on PBS from time to time, but Americans basically look at their own programming. They have no understanding or concept or sensitivity to a country such as ours, where 98 per cent of our drama is from a foreign country and, therefore, we have to provide protection. They see it purely as something that is a market-place decision, a market-place decision, by the way, that must be buttressed and supported by the power of the state.
I am just illustrating this particular observation that was made to me. It is one reason why the Americans have been so supportive of this particular trade agreement. They see it as a
Broadcasting Act
way of establishing a precedent for bludgeoning into other markets around the world.
The attitude expressed by Secretary Treasurer Baker and Ambassador Yeutter in front of the House of Representatives and the Senate Committee, on testifying, shows very clearly that the reason that American Congressmen should support the trade legislation is that it will give a lesson to other countries, that if they try to get cute on things like culture, establishing new forums and relations, then the Canadian example can be used to break through.
They will be using this, very clearly, as part of their argument at the Uruguay Round to open up the whole system around the world for their access, because they know that they have such a dominant position in order to be able to do this. Attempts by other countries to provide content provisions or limitations will now be under attack, and we are aiding and abetting in that attack by the acquiescence of the trade agreement.
This is not simply a matter of a debate between some cultural groups. This is part of a very clear and broad trade strategy by the United States. They are under pressure and they are losing markets in their manufacturing, and they see that the opportunities in the service industries and to the so-called entertainment industry is prime among those. They will be using this in a way that they hope will bash their way in to other world markets. Other countries have attempted to preserve their cultural arrangements against that kind of Americanization. We are in fact an accomplice to something that will become a very major and dramatic debate, the GATT Round, and unfortunately we are on the wrong side of the argument.

Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in this debate, although I didn't think it would be necessary. I thought the Government would understand the incredible significance of this debate. What I fail to understand, Madam Speaker, is that during the last minutes of a reign, of a government, we are . ..
Filibuster!

I beg your pardon. If you really think this is a filibuster, you don't know what a filibuster is, because if anyone can organize a filibuster, I certainly can and I would give you your money's worth! I regret the attitude of the Hon. Member for . . . for which riding?
Are you objecting to the fact that some of our Members have the right to speak on broadcasting? Is that your complaint, Madam Minister? Ridiculous.

Right. So if we can let bygones be bygones, the Minister seems very anxious to have her Bill adopted, and I understand that. The Minister would like to see

September 27, 1988
Broadcasting Act
her legislation passed as quickly as possible. Elowever, Madam Speaker, we are talking about some vital issues. As an experienced parliamentarian, I fail to understand that having come to the very end of this Government's mandate-of course this Government was duly and democratically elected, I realize that-I can't understand why, within the last two weeks, this Government has introduced bills that are incredibly important to Canada's future. There was the child care Bill, which of course is not before the House today, Madam Speaker.
I briefly took part in it, not on the substance of the matter but on the way we were to vote on it. It is as though the Government, at the last minute, looked back on its election platform of four years and two months ago and said, "Oh, how can it be? We forgot day care! Let's bring in a Bill, rush the Opposition, rush all the interest groups and pass this Bill." In the last minute, almost at the last gasp of a dying Parliament! And again today, they come to us with a Bill! I see that they are impatient, that the Minister is very impatient, I understand that, but if she would bear with us, I could tell her, "Madam, why did you not force your Government to deal with this question long before today?"
When you have a Minister with clout in a department or in Cabinet, I think it is that Minister's duty, as my colleague, the Whip for my Party, and my Party's excellent critic, the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), will tell you, when a Minister has clout, he or she must fight within Cabinet and say, "This is a priority." If it is a priority today, in the last minute, why were these Bills not a priority a year ago?
So I am quite amazed that in the last minute, perhaps in the last week of a long reign, because their term in office is almost the equivalent of five years, Madam, since we have sat continually, with extended hours and summer leave cancelled. The Government has really had five years and not four and in the very last minute, it wants to force through two bills that it considers very important and that we consider important. It wants to show Canadians that the Opposition is blocking two Bills, when there have only been three speakers, I think, on this Bill.. . Madam Speaker, I will not participate in a filibuster. We know that! I believe in Parliamentary reform. But I can tell you one thing: there is a difference between what you call a filibuster in English, i.e. unduly prolonging debate, and not debating at all, and we are within those limits.
You know, Madam Speaker, that we attach great importance to this Bill-that is understandable. Why? Because today, what is Canadians' main activity? It is watching television. It is not playing sports. Canadians are glued to the television twenty-four hours a week on average. It is important to know what is on television. It is important to know who controls television. Every year, for our young pages who have just arrived . . .
Our young pages who have just arrived are a product of that generation. Each year Canadian children watch almost 1,000 hours of television, compared to 800 hours spent in school.
It reminds me of the debate I had some years ago when I had the honour of being the arts and culture critic prior to my esteemed colleague, the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), who did a remarkable job in her new assignment. I remember that I said to the Hon. Member for Frontenac (Mr. Masse) when he was the Minister, and that was before he became popular, "You have a duty, Mr. Minister. You are not the defender of cabinet decisions near the artist, you have the duty to defend the artist in Cabinet." That is my conception of a Minister.

That is how I see a Minister's responsibility. He has a duty to defend the interests of his sector, meaning that if I am Minister of Youth, I defend youth, and if I am Minister of Seniors, I passionately defend senior citizens, and I would certainly do that. If I am supposed to defend farmers, I have a duty to stand up to my Cabinet colleagues. I am not supposed to take the Cabinet's decisions and get them accepted by the people whose interests I am supposed to represent. It wouldn't make sense.
I repeat what I said earlier that our children, who will build the Canada of tomorrow, watch 1000 hours of television and spend only 800 hours in school.
Madam Speaker, 95 per cent of Canadians listen to the radio for an average 18 hours a week. Madam Speaker, this is very, very significant, if my figures are correct.
But I said all this during the debate we had two and a half years ago to Mr. Masse, our present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Two-thirds of Canadians . . .

Two-thirds of Canadians admit that watching television is their favourite pastime. I enjoy it too. Sometimes I watch television for too long in the late hours and it is terrible, Madam Speaker, as you know very well when you have to get up early in the morning, and you cannot do otherwise but keep watching television because it is interesting. In my case I watch international affairs, disarmament questions, east-west relationships, and political programs; for others it is a cowboy program, a criminal program, or violence. However, it is very important.
Today we are told we are filibustering after three speakers. We must make sure Canadians understand, regardless of whether or not there is an an election coming that, at the very last minute this Government has decided today to ram through the House a very major, capital, and important piece of legislation. That is the reason that, at the very last minute, I accepted the request of my esteemed colleague, the Hon.
September 27, 1988

Member for Mount Royal, who did a remarkable job in participating in this debate.
Fifty per cent of Canadians say that they are not too interested in reading, that their principal source of news and information comes from broadcasting. Madam Speaker, can you imagine that 50 per cent of Canadians say that broadcasting is their principal source of news and information. What does that mean in practice? It means that television shapes the minds of the people. Television shows them the type of news, or does not show them the type of news, and this is very dangerous. You, Madam Speaker, know what 1 am talking about because of your great career prior to this career. You understand the importance of broadcasting and television.
These young people who have just arrived to work in Parliament are the ones who probably tomorrow will be sitting in the House of Commons. Some of them get their information from television, or they are influenced by television. When you have a neighbour like the United States of America, and I hope they are listening across the street-for the time being. For listeners, when I say "across the street", I have to explain, to have an intelligent debate, that it is because the Embassy of the United States of America is across the street here in Ottawa.
When I was a student it used to be called the American Embassy. I remember I lead a delegation-I always liked demonstrations what I was a student. We had a few demonstrations to tell them that they should not call themselves the American Embassy, but the Embassy of the United States of America. It was a nuance that we students understood. We were proud Canadians and we understood the difference, because we are part of America too, but we are not citizens of the United States of America. We are Canadian. If we want to remain Canadian, if we want to have a Canadian country, and if we want to progress toward the future in remaining what we are and in becoming even better, we have to watch how we shape our brains. You do this by what you listen to, by what you see, or by what you read. It so happens that Canadians prefer television to reading. That means you gradually form an opinion of the world, of Canada, of your province, of your own race or religion, by what influences you. I repeat that to make Canadians understand why at this very last minute, it is important that we do not deal with this Bill urgently.
Last week it was day care. We are supposed to have a new era in Canada of participatory parliamentary process. Members of Parliament would be more independent. They would be somebodies after all. You remember that famous quote. Parliamentarians thought they were going to be somebody. They were going to give their time, their devotion, their patience and their understanding in working in a parliamentary committee. This was the invention of the man who is now Lieutenant Governor of Newfoundland. He put his name on the report, the McGrath report. That dealt with reform of the House of Commons and its committees.
Broadcasting Act
What happened with day care? Some 40 witnesses said it was bad, it was wrong. They are all experts. I am not an expert on day care, but I recognize its immense importance. You may smile but I understand the problems if we do not take care of our young Canadians. They are raised differently than you and I were raised. They are raised differently than my esteemed colleague from Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) was raised. Today we have a lot of single parents who could go on welfare. They want to work but they have children. They need day care. This did not exist in my day. I am the youngest of 12 children. We did not have day care because our society was different. I know we need a good full day care system, yet we rammed the Bill through the House. We did not listen to anything that was said in the committee. Now it has gone to the Senate and the Government would like the Senate to ram it through, otherwise the Conservatives will campaign against those in the Senate.
I say to the Senators: "As long as you exist, do your duty. You have the duty to at least study the Bill, at least for a couple of days. At least three days." Is that asking too much for something that is supposed to cost $6.4 billion?
Amendments to this Bill here today were turned down. Why did my colleague from Mount Royal work so hard? It is because she believed in the spirit of the McGrath report that says legislative committees will have some power. Power to convince. Power to be convinced. Power to call Canadians to participate, to give us their view, and then react accordingly.
There are parliamentarians who are stubborn and say this is the Bill, the Queen can do no wrong, the Minister can do no wrong, and it is take it or leave it. I would rather say leave it for a while until we come to our senses and recognize that the Bill is too important to ram it through the House so rapidly.
Do I need to say that the broadcasting message very often is not Canadian? I could talk for hours about Canada. Yes, I become passionate. What the hell am I doing in the House of Commons if I do not believe in Canada? I came here for that. Everything that could help us frame a good Canada must be debated and understood. Programming must be Canadian.
We should also remember it is all very well to talk about anglophones and francophones but we must understand that long before we were here, long before even my ancestors came to this country in the 1600s, there were native people and we should address that question.
1 also disagree with the role of the President and Chairman of the CBC. This should be addressed.
I must conclude by saying I am disappointed, as Canadians should be, that a sense of urgency seems to have fallen upon the House of Commons. Everything is urgent. There is no urgency. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) can call the election in the spring if he has such a-
No.

Why not? I do not mind.

Broadcasting Act
I would like to conclude by saying that this Bill should be suspended. If it is the intention of the Prime Minister of Canada, as is his right, to call an election, day care and this legislation should be put on the shelf and left to the next Government to decide how it wants to tackle it.
