Madam Speaker, as the critic for communications and culture but more importantly as a Canadian, I know the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) has a very passionate sense of the place of Canada and the importance of maintaining our identity. I heard him extol, and rightly so, the importance of differentiating ourselves from our American friends and cousins. He very often says that good fences make good neighbours.
Given that, I wonder how he feels about the fact that this Bill, while purportedly saying we are going to have a better Canadian broadcasting system, allows all kinds of American programs to come in here unlicensed. It does not define the necessity for predominantly Canadian content. It does not say where that content should appear on the screen.
The Hon. Member has also been outspoken, certainly in the lobby, with respect to TV5 and its importance for all Canadians. Therefore, does he feel it would be fair to allow the American systems access to our market and have them take the money out and produce fine programming but programming which can be hurtful to Canadian artists and their potential to grow and reach the world class level they are capable of?

Well, Madam Speaker, that will show to my friend that we did not prepare ourselves accordingly, because if we had, I would be able to pick up a paper and have the answer. I will try. This is exactly what Winston Churchill said. This is true parliamentary debate and exchange. The essence of the British parliamentary system is to have that kind of exchange, unprepared. We see from time to time one of the members of the majority in the House asking a question of the Minister, such as happened today, and the Minister rising and giving the answer. Everyone knows it is theatre, it is prepared.
I do not deny the fact that Americans produce good programs. Of course, they do. They are so rich and powerful. I can use the same argument for the trade agreement of the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and of President Reagan. I do not deny the fact that the Americans produce big and produce good, but they are big. I am not afraid of that. I enjoy the neighbourhood of the United States. I enjoy everything it can offer me, as I would hope Americans would enjoy what we can offer them. Unfortunately, it is very often a one-way street. The United States is so big. It does not want to harm us. I am sure of that. I am absolutely friendly with the United States of America. But I know one thing, being big as
September 27, 1988
it is, it cannot care less about what it does to us, and this immense invasion of programming reduces our Canadianism. There is no doubt about that. Canadians will have to decide what kind of country they want and what kind of Canadianism they want to give to those who will come after them.
I am always extremely suspicious when a Bill of this kind is too general in tone. I do not like too much regulation. But there is not enough protection for us in this Bill against the absolute infiltration by American programming. It is not bad, it is dangerous, and at least we should realize it is dangerous. In a country the size of Canada, with our small population, we have to double our efforts in being more careful when we arrive at something that goes directly to the fabric of Canada, and that is this Bill. It is-

It is vague. It is not specific. There are too many loopholes. I am not overly fond of Bills that tell me where I am supposed to put the stamp on the envelope, and I hope I didn't give that impression. The simili, in any case, is very French. However, I would like to know how we can protect ourselves against this huge giant, a giant I am quite fond of, and I am referring to the United States. They are so pervasive and so powerful that if we don't watch out, the situation might become very dangerous for us.

What do we see in the national anthem? I had the honour, under the Right Hon. Lester Pearson, to be appointed to the National Anthem Committee. The Hon. Member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) and I are the only sitting Members left of that committee. What did we include in the English version of O Canadal We say: "We stand on guard for thee". What does it mean? It means we must be careful with a Bill of this kind.

We must watch out. In fact, the same would apply, as I said earlier, to the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. The agreement is not all bad.

We have what the Government calls the Free Trade Agreement, or, as my Party prefers to call it, the Mulroney-Reagan agreement. It would be silly to say that everything in it is bad.
I am not ready to say that. I did not say it and I will not say it. But I am allowed to "stand on guard for thee". I say to you, the young people, it is your Canada that is at stake in the trade agreement. It is your Canada that is at stake in the kind of day care we want for Canada. It is your Canada that is at stake with these kinds of Bills, especially this one. This Bill is the most important thing because this is what influences people. How can we be denied the right to debate a little longer than three or four speakers for something that is-

.. . that goes straight to the roots of our Canadian identity?
I am certainly not ashamed of taking part in the debate at the
September 27, 1988

very last minute, because I thought the Government would say: Listen, we are going to call an election, enough is enough!

Enough is enough. How many more Bills does my dear friend have up his sleeve to try to ram through the House? Is he going to bring in Bill C-79? I had the honour to be the Chairman of the legislative committee on the reform of the Election Act. Is he going to bring another Bill forward? I would say, please, Madam Speaker, enough is enough. Please let us study this more attentively.

Madam Speaker, thank you, for giving me this opportunity to speak in debate on this important piece of legislation. One of the most important aspects of this present crisis in Canadian broadcasting is the increasing continentalization of our airwaves. The all-Party standing committee in its report recognized this problem and made a number of strong recommendations to ensure the distinctiveness of the Canadian market. These were not minor recommendations. As the sixth report of the standing committee, chaired by Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Edwards), noted, these recommendations were parallel in importance to the Canadian content requirements that apply to individual licensed broadcasters. It is a combination of the Canadian content obligations applying to individual broadcasters and the carriage priorities, and other carriage rules applicable to cable, that determine whether the Canadian programming objectives set out in the broadcasting policy can be met.
The Minister explicitly rejected these recommendations to create a distinctive Canadian market. For example, Recommendation 58 said that the Act should be drafted so as to define the essential role of the distribution undertakings as that of distributing Canadian radio and television services in French and in English, both public and private, with first priority given to the public sector Canadian services, followed by private Canadian services.
With the exception of the three-plus-one services already carried, the Act should make provision for the carriage of foreign radio and television services only when the programming they provide is complimentary to that available from licensed Canadian broadcasters and network operators. The Act should also provide for priority to be given to the carriage of services in French and distribution undertakings that serve primarily Francophone subscribers.
Clearly it is the result of the trade deal negotiations that has hamstrung the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald). My colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver- Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), put forward two motions that
Broadcasting Act
reflected the standing committee's and task force's reports to amend this Bill at report stage. They were Motions Nos. 36 and 39.
Motion No. 36 would ensure that all services operating in Canada, including U.S. satellite-to-cable services, are licensed. The House knows, for example, that the U.S. Arts and Entertainment Network is beamed into Canada by satellite and affiliates with cable companies package and sell it to Canadian subscribers. It makes no contribution to Canadian programming and does not need to meet the requirements of the CRTC. In fact, it basically costs A & E nothing to tap the Canadian market.
As the Association of Canadian Film and Television Producers said before the standing committee:
It would be consistent with the government's stated policies for broadcasting in Canada to require all broadcast services available in Canada to be subject to CRTC regulation and approval. The CRTC has a demonstrated sensibility to the needs of broadcasters and the government's policy priorities. We should all be confident in the Commission's ability to develop a realistic licensing process for foreign satellite-to-cable services coming into Canada, given a solid legislative base.
That is what Motion No. 36 sought to do.
More important than this, however, was Motion No. 39. This motion would have ensured that, with the exception of the three plus one American networks, NBC, CBS, ABC and PBS and border stations, that carriage of foreign stations should only be provided by cable systems if the programming they provide is complementary to that available from licensed Canadian broadcasters and network operations. This motion is in part a response to the continuing penetration into the Canadian cable market by U.S. services. In particular, I am referring to the recent decision to license U.S. superstations which provide the unique service of Beverley Hillbilly reruns 12 hours a day in addition to Atlanta Braves, Mets and other baseball games.
As the producer groups rightly said when they came before the legislative committee, this will have a highly negative effect on the ability of Canadian producers to maintain a distinct Canadian market. To quote Sam Jephcott of the CFTA:
Canadian producers have relied on the "cordon sanitaire" that kept such channels out of Canada in the past, an advantage that allowed them to license original Canadian programming to Canadian broadcasters as well as American ones, without the diminution in value that inevitably occurs when market exclusivity is compromised by transborder signal penetration.
Just as important as the question of a distinct Canadian production market is that of the viability of Canadian local stations such as City TV and specialty stations in the face of competition from directly competing U.S. services.
As I noted earlier, this motion comes from a direct communication of the all-Party standing committee's sixth report. In her response to that report, tabled with this Bill, the Minister gave the following reply, which is in my mind really quite extraordinary:

September 27, 1988
Broadcasting Act
The prohibition of foreign radio and television services other than those whose programming is complementary to that available from Canadian broadcasters has not been included in the legislation, since it would unduly restrict Canadians' access to a range of international broadcasting services.
The impact of the Minister's policy is really something quite different. She is simply dead wrong. Her policy will limit Canadian choices and the chance to watch Canadian broadcast services. As the Friends of Canadian Broadcasting rightly put it:
If this country had adopted such an approach 60 years ago this country would never have developed a separate Canadian broadcasting system except in the public sector.
We are not proposing to stop Canadians from getting complementary services. We just want Canadians to have the chance to provide them. The standing committee, in the sixth report, put it very well, I think, by saying:
We note that even in the large U.S. market, where service is provided entirely in English, there is only one available service in most programming categories. In Canada, it is beyond question that a Canadian service could not co-exist with a non-Canadian service, especially if the Canadian service is expected to provide a meaningful contribution to Canadian programming.
There was a Conservative majority on that committee, so the question is, what made the Tories-I notice one or two around-change their minds? Well, a group called the Cultural Industries Alliance made up of more than a dozen major cultural organizations has said the following:
We have already seen evidence of the effect of the trade agreement on existing policies and policy development. This includes the rejection of key recommendation for Broadcast Policy made by the House of Commons Standing Committee-
This brings us to the general question of the impact of this trade deal on our cultural industries. It has clearly had an impact on the Bill before us. The Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) trade deal threatens to change completely the nature of cultural activity in Canada. The Prime Minister has repeatedly claimed that cultural policy was untouched by the trade deal. He has said with apparent pride that the status quo has been maintained.
What is the nature of the status quo of which the Prime Minister is so proud? Only 3 per cent of film profits stay in Canada, 3 per cent of videocassette sales are Canadian, prime time drama is 2 per cent to 3 per cent Canadian, and 77 per cent of all magazines sold in Canada are of foreign origin. The litany of statistics goes on. No other sovereign country can match this unfortunate situation.
The fact is that the United States has succeeded, in the trade negotiations, in whittling away at Canada's cultural programs as it has whittled away at so much of the character of Canada. As a direct or indirect result of the trade deal talks, the Conservative administration has abandoned its film distribution policy, abandoned the Baie Comeau book publishing policy which sought to repatriate a portion of our publishing industry, reduced the capital cost allowance on Canadian films which the Americans had argued was an unfair subsidy, and rejected a number of important recommendations of the House of Commons standing committee in the
recently announced broadcasting policy. Worse, the trade deal effectively blocks Canada from adopting new policies to reverse the foreign domination of our culture so clearly revealed in the above-mentioned statistics.
According to Trade Ambassador Simon Reisman, new measures affecting cultural industries would be scrutinized by both sides to determine whether they are consistent or inconsistent with the agreement. The United States will be able to take retaliatory action of "equivalent commercial effect" against any Canadian cultural program that is inconsistent in its view with the agreement. In effect, it defines as an unjust cultural subsidy any action which costs the United States money.
In the area of communication as in so many other spheres of our relationship with the United States as a result of the trade deal, we are chipping away at the character of Canada and chipping away at those structures which will enable us to determine our own future, not only in the economic sphere but in the cultural sphere as well. What is more, we add to the sad litany of negative effects for our country that have been listed by those of us who oppose this deal.
I was interested in hearing my colleague in the Liberal Party express his pride in our country. That is a pride that I would like to have maintained in my own heart. However, that kind of pride in this country can only be reinforced and maintained if we have those powers and those abilities within our land that will enable us to determine our own future in all spheres, not because we are disinterested in appropriate economic and commercial relationships with other countries but because, if we are to have proper and rewarding relationships with other countries, as other countries have with us, those relationships must be based on the integrity of our nationhood.
This Bill, as so many others, because of a context which chips away at that nationhood, constitutes a failure on the part of the Government that should be the basis for its punishment when after Friday afternoon the Prime Minister, we all hope, will finally get up the courage to go to the polls to determine whether in fact the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal will be the determinant of our future or whether it will be the consciences and the needs of the Canadian people which will determine the future of our country.
Mir. Allmand: Mr. Speaker, in his speech the Hon. Member has stated that this Conservative Broadcasting Act will threaten the capacity of Canada to project its individuality, its soul, its self and, in particular, its capacity to project that individuality up against this massive attack of American media which comes from south of the border to threaten, not intentionally, I believe, Canadian expression or Canadian culture. However, it is a massive attack of radio, television, magazines, and even newspapers. Today I was walking down the street and saw that we now have newspaper boxes for U.S.
September 27, 1988

News Today on our streets. That may become more prevalent if this free trade deal goes into operation.
The Member has very well expressed this threat to our capacity, through broadcasting, to express ourselves as Canadians. I want to make sure that his point is not missed by the Canadian electorate who might be following this debate. Could he give us some more examples of exactly how threatening this Bill is to our capacity to do that. We do not get too many opportunities to put forward our point of view. We do not have the same resources as the Government, and I look on these debates in the House of Commons as one of the few means that we have to expose the weaknesses of the Government's legislation.
I know the Member ran out of time. Perhaps he has some more examples of how serious a threat this Bill is to broadcasting in Canada and the capacity of our country to express its culture and individuality so that we all have something in common.

Madam Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for the question. I was much taken with the preamble to his question in which he cited the tremendous impact upon Canadian culture of the American media. I immediately began to reflect upon that most conspicuous of matters treated in recent weeks by the American media, to wit, the presidential election. I like to think of Canada as a tolerant country, a country that accepts dissent, accepts a diversity of opinion. Indeed, I would like to think of Canada as-and please do not misunderstand me, let me make sure that I say this clearly- essentially a small "1" liberal country. I mean that to construe a nation of tolerance, of diversity of ideas and dissent.
We are being bombarded with the notion that somehow it is a sin to be a liberal by an American media which, through this Bill will gain, one way or another, continued and perhaps expanded access to Canada as an audience. It is suggested that to believe seriously that sticking laser weapons and other kinds of contraptions in orbit for war purposes is destabilizing, and to describe it as such and to suggest for a moment that these mass expenditures on weapons constitute a danger to society is somehow bad. They suggest that if every American does not, at every excuse, jump up and recite the Pledge of Allegiance, that is somehow un-American.
I know, Madam Speaker, that just as I and my colleague from Vancouver-Kingsway, you have been aware of what is going on there. That is an election that is based on the notion that a good society is an intolerant society. This may seem like a small thing but I think that most Canadians, were they to realize that this pervasive encroachment of the American media and those kinds of American attitudes have a serious impact on our young people, would be offended by it if they examined it for just a moment.
Surely it is significant to our country that those attitudes, which have developed in another nation with a history quite different from ours, should become determinant in our own
Broadcasting Act
attitudes in a country which I consider to be one of the more civilized countries in the world. Inevitably, if we do not enhance the opportunity for Canadians to have greater and greater access to those attitudes which are the foundation of our nation, our nation will be threatened seriously.
I find it offensive to have a trade deal that says that if we attempt to increase the degree to which we communicate our values through our cultural media there will be retaliation from our trading partner, the partner in the economic agreement. That, all by itself, is sufficient reason for rejecting the trade deal.
I do not know whether, in expressing this concern, I have specifically answered the question of my respected colleague, but I thank him for the opportunity to allow me to point out the real impact that the present debate in the United States has on our country through the American media. More important, the content of that debate is so destructive, so pitiful in its disregard even for American values, that I fear the penetration of such a set of values in our own country. Without any means of limiting it, it promises difficulties for us in the future.

Madam Speaker, I know you are a much younger person than am I, but I would like you to cast your mind back a few years to remember the first time you or your family owned a television set. If you can remember those days perhaps you can also remember how you got the reception on that set in those days. I know that you have appeared on television yourself many times since then, Madam Speaker, and you are appearing on television right now. I would like you to cast your mind back a year or two to those days when the first television set was acquired in your family and to think of exactly how you got your reception in those days. That is the picture I would like you to have in your mind as I make my comments this evening.
I do not know what you remember about that, Madam Speaker, but I remember quite vividly when my family got our first television set. We had an aerial on the roof. There were some guy wires attached to that aerial to hold it on the roof. They were wrapped around some screws that were sunk in the roof. Sometimes when the wind blew one wondered whether the aerial would come down. Of course, the reception on the television was not very good. After a few years water began to leak where those screws were sunk into the roof. It was not a very satisfactory method of getting television reception.
When my wife and I got our first home, I was rather pleased that it did not have one of these aerials on the roof. It had a big tower on the side of the house. I remember those days very well, when there was a tower up the side of the house on which there was a television aerial. That is how we used to get our signals for television reception.
That was fine in our family for a while, but one day, not too long after we moved into our house, our three-year old

September 27, 1988
Broadcasting Act
daughter, Kim, was playing in the yard. My wife and I were looking out the back window from the second story and suddenly a face appeared at this window. It was our three-year old daughter, Kim, who climbed up the television tower and was looking in the window at us. As a result of that we decided that that was not a very good way of getting our television reception either and in fact it would be better to make a deal with a cable company and have them string some cable into the house to get our reception that way.
That is the way many people, particularly in urban centres, get their television coverage these days. When you become a cable subscriber sometimes you feel a little as though you might be a captive of the cable company, perhaps a captive of the CRTC because the CRTC regulates the cable companies and allots the territorial franchises for those companies so that there is inevitably just one cable company where you live. You must buy your television signal from one television cable company and you do not have any choice. As a result of that the companies can dictate the kind of programming you get. They set the rate for the cost of that programming and, of course, they do that in conjunction with the CRTC that regulates those companies. That programming is set in a way that sometimes we do not always appreciate.
I do not know whether you have heard from your constituents on that subject but I have heard a lot from my constituency in the last few months about changes in the kinds of stations that are now being received and changes in the rates being charged. Senior citizens in particular, who watch a lot of television, feel rather upset and concerned that they are being dictated to by the cable companies and the CRTC.
People who live in a single family home have another alternative to a cable company. It is the satellite television receiver by which people can bring in signals from everywhere. They do not have to rely on a cable television operation and do not have to pay the cable company. They are not a captive of cable television because they have the right to install their own dish in their own yard.
The interesting part of the satellite receiver is that it is not regulated by this Bill we are discussing this evening, Bill C-136. The Bill exempts from regulation an individual homeowner who might want to put a satellite dish in his or her yard. Individual homeowners like me and others are not governed by the provisions of this Bill. We do not stand to be regulated or licensed. We do not stand to pay a fee. In fact, this Bill exempts single family homeowners specifically from that kind of regulation.
However, people who live in a condominium apartment or townhouse, who are homeowners just like individuals in a single family detached dwelling, would not have an alternative to cable television. They would become subscribers to cable and subject to all those rules and regulations of cable. They could be subject to having to buy the same kind of programming that those cable companies give to everyone else. They could be subject to paying the fees and the increased fees each
year that cable companies seek and which seem to be inevitably approved by the CRTC. They do not have an alternative of a dish or satellite television receiver that a single family detached homeowner would have, unless it was regulated.
The Bill we are discussing tonight regulates condominiums. It does not specifically exempt them from the provisions of the Bill as it does with single family homeowners. That is discriminatory. People who live in condominium apartments and townhouses feel very keenly that they are being discriminated against by this Bill. It is true that if each condominium owner decided to own his or her own satellite dish they would not be regulated. If there was a complex with 40 units and there was a dish on each of the 40 balconies or 40 dishes sitting on the roof, they would not be regulated. They would be considered to be exempt under the terms of the Bill.
However, because there may only be one, two or perhaps three dishes for the whole complex, whether they be town-houses or apartments that are owned just like you or I own a single home, they are subject to regulation. They are subject to be licensed and pay fees. It is not so much that condominium owners feel it is wrong to pay fees, wrong to be regulated or wrong to be licensed, but that they should be treated exactly the same as owners of single family dwellings. I agree with them very strongly. Otherwise, they are being discriminated against.
Condominium owners have gone through this battle many times in the past. They have gone through this battle with respect to property taxes. The House may be aware of the appeals that have been taken by condominium owners against assessments for municipal property taxes based on the fact of discrimination, on the fact that originally when all these condominium complexes were assessed for real estate taxes on a municipal basis they were assessed on the same basis as if they were a business, not as if they were single homes. They were assessed as if they were generating some sort of profit out of this. As a result, they were given the same type of assessment that a rental apartment building would have been given, a building in which there is an owner and tenants, in which the owner charges not only rent to cover the costs but to make a profit.
Condominium complexes originally, and there are probably some still today, were assessed on the same basis because they look like an apartment complex. They were assessed on the same basis as an apartment complex with the assumption that there was some sort of a business profit being generated. It was thought they should have a higher assessment than your home, Madam Speaker, and mine, a single-family detached dwelling.
Of course, condominium owners fought against this and fought against it very hard. There were appeals one after another in my province from city to city, from neighbourhood to neighbourhood, from complex to complex. Eventually, in
September 27, 1988

most cases, certainly in my own constituency, those condominium owners were successful in having their assessments reduced to something comparable to that of your home and mine, Madam Speaker, single-family detached homes and dwellings.
They have been used to this sort of discrimination between single-family home owners and condominium owners over many, many years. They do not like it. It is quite natural that they do not like it. That is why they are upset with this Bill, just in the same way that they were upset with their real estate taxes many years ago, and perhaps to some extent upset with them today because of that discrimination.
You may or may not be aware, Madam Speaker, that many of these complexes were discriminated against, as some undoubtedly are today as well, as far as garbage collection is concerned. Once again municipalities treated them as if they were a profit centre, as if they were a business, as if they were an apartment building with an owner who was generating some profits. The concept for many years with those types of buildings was: "Look, we will charge you some taxes. The taxes may be higher than you might otherwise pay if this were a single home, but you will have to pay this high rate of taxes, and there are certain services we will supply you with". One of those services was garbage collection.
The garbage truck, sanitary engineers from the municipality, did not go around to the apartment buildings to pick up the garbage. That was not part of the tax bill. That was an extra that the apartment owners had to arrange for, had to pay for separately apart from regular garbage collection service. He or she then had to charge that back to the tenant and increase the rents in order to do so. It was the same concept that municipalities originally took with respect to condominiums, whether it be an apartment complex or townhouse complex. It was the same theory that was applied, which was that condominiums are a different sort of animal from the single-family detached home.
Condominium owners fought against that kind of discrimination as well. Eventually, they won, at least in my constituency and in my municipality. They may still be fighting those battles in some other municipalities across the country, but in mine they won.
It is against this background of discrimination, this background of a matter of high principle for condominium owners, a principle which says that they should be treated exactly the same as any other home owner, that they view this Bill. They view it as gross discrimination against them as condominium owners.
This piece of legislation and the particular problem of discriminating against condominium owners with respect to television reception in terms of satellite TV receivers did not start today. It did not start with this Bill. It did not start four years ago with this Government. Quite frankly, it started many years ago with the former Government, the Liberal Government, and the Broadcasting Act which this Bill is aimed at amending and replacing. That sort of discrimination between
Broadcasting Act
single-family home owners and condominium owners was inherent in that legislation, as well as in the legislation that was put in place by the former Liberal Government. Condominium owners did not just suddenly rear up and get excited when they saw this Bill for the first time as it concerns this issue. This is an issue that has been going on with them for years and years. In fact, it has been going on since the early eighties at least.
I recall that when I first made it known that I was going to be standing for Parliament in the last election, representatives of condominium complexes in my riding came to me. They outlined the problem for me and showed me the problem that was in the present legislation that had been put in place by the former Government. They said: "For Heaven's sake, we are counting on you. We are counting on a new Progressive Conservative Government to correct this wrong and to make sure that there is no discrimination in the future".
I took that message and conveyed it to the then Leader of the Official Opposition, the Present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). I conveyed it to him in the form of letters that I wrote to him. I conveyed it to him in private meetings. As you may recall, Madam Speaker, I have conveyed it to him publicly in this House during this debate, the debates that have preceded this one and in statements that I have made in the House pursuant to Standing Order 21.
I have tried my best to get the message across that what the Government is doing here is viewed very vehemently and strongly by condominium owners not only in my riding but across Canada as gross discrimination.
I would like to add here that about 5 per cent of the population of Canada-5 per cent of the 25 million or 26 million who live in this country-live in condominiums. We are talking about something in excess of one million people who are potentially affected by this provision in the Bill, a million people in the country who feel that they are discriminated against as a result of this Bill.
It was not just with the Prime Minister that I expressed these concerns. I expressed them with every Minister of Communications and Culture that we have had since the Government took office in 1984. I have had meetings with those Ministers. I have had meetings with their exempt staff and their political staff. I have had meetings with their department officials. I have had meetings separately on my own and I have had meetings collectively with numerous other Members of Parliament who share this concern that I have on behalf of our constituents. It would seem that they have all been to no avail.
Initially, it appeared that we were making progress. You will recall, Madam Speaker, that early on in the mandate of the Government there was another Bill concerning broadcasting, Bill C-20. That particular Bill had inherent in it the same discrimination aspects as this Bill has with respect to condominium owners.

September 27, 1988
Broadcasting Act
It was as a result of that particular piece of legislation and the meetings that took place around it within the Progressive Conservative caucus that an organization called the backbench committee was formed. It is a committee which has been subject to a great deal of discussion, a great deal of debate. Some people, including my friend from Ottawa- Vanier, has characterized it as the dinosaur club of the Progressive Conservative Party. If we are the dinosaurs of the Progressive Conservative Party, we were born as a result of concern arising out of this issue, the issue of cable television, broadcasting, et cetera.
What has to happen is that we must have some changes made to this Bill or we have to see it die. That is what happened to Bill C-20. It died on the Order Paper when the first session of the Thirty-third Parliament came to an end. That Bill was allowed by the Government to die on the Order Paper. At that time it had apparently seen the light. But it did not because subsequently, as we can see, there was this new Bill, Bill C-136. Here we are at third reading. There are a great many people-over one million-in the country who are condominium owners who would like to see this Bill die on the Order Paper. Quite frankly, that is their last hope, their last gasp.
I see that you are giving me the time signal, Madam Speaker, but I hope perhaps somebody will ask me a question and allow me to make one or two further points.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Member got my attention when he mentioned my riding of Ottawa-Vanier and referred to my identifying some members of his caucus as dinosaurs. At the time I thought that indeed on the language issue, on Bill C-72, the people who were and are opposing certain amendments to the law of the land were indeed people who spoke of prior times or who represented possibly some thoughts or some trends that were with us many years ago, but he has now enlightened me by telling me that indeed it started with the back-bench committee. I remember that one too, so I thank him for reminding me of the historical significance of the dinosaur dynasty in the Progressive Conservative Party.
I know that the Member has a great interest in the condominium question on Bill C-136. I know that he has had a number of constituents call and write to him, and he has made us aware of the numerous interventions of his constituents.
He is certainly aware that our concerns have been similar to his in dealing with the wording of the definition of "distribution undertaking" in Clause 2(1), which, when taken together with Clause 4(3), would clearly bring the MATV, the master of TV systems, under the Act to the extent that they receive and distribute broadcast signals.
I want to quote something from the Canadian Bar Association's brief which I have before me and which impressed me as being somewhat enlightening and revealing of what, I would suppose, a very good body of lawyers would have to say about
the subject of Bill C-136. I may want to ask the Member to comment on that.
They state in their brief to the legislative committee on Bill C-136, "There continues to be an omission in the Act, namely the situation where an apartment or hotel distribution system, either using encrypted radio signals or a closed circuit cable system, provides programs solely to the tenants of the apartment building or the guest rooms of an hotel. Constitutional issues aside, in that case, the new Act would not apply to the system because the signals would probably not be thought of as being intended for reception by the public". That is the end of the quote from the testimony of the Canadian Bar Association.
I wonder if the Member, who I think has a good background in law-1 do not know if he is a lawyer, but he impresses me sometimes with his arguments-could explain to us if he has had any representations or comments from lawyers dealing maybe with the legalistic point of view here. It may be narrower than saying, as he has been telling us in the House, that indeed we should treat condominium owners as singledwelling property owners are treated, that is, having the right to utilize the MATV systems.
I wonder if he could bring us up to date on the legal approaches to this Bill. Is he satisfied, for example, that there is a fuzziness to the Bill that would make it possible for a court to have to pass judgment on the interpretations of these clauses, and is there a danger that we are indeed going to be finding ourselves in a legal mess, in a few months or a few years down the road, with this wording of the definition of distribution undertaking, in Clauses 2(1) and 4(3)?

Madam Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) for his comments. I might say that the Canadian Bar Association's brief and their comments were made to the legislative committee dealing with this Bill before amendments were made to that clause that the Hon. Member referred to, the distribution undertaking clause.
In that committee, on the clause-by-clause passage of the Bill, there was an amendment made to this clause, as the Hon. Member knows, which added to the end of the definition of distribution undertaking the words "or dwelling unit, or to another such undertaking".
The purpose of that amendment, of course, was to try to solve the problem that had been pointed out by the Bar Association and raised by the Hon. Member, to take the fuzziness out of that definition. But in taking the fuzziness out of the definition, it in fact made it quite clear, in the eyes of the lawyers for the Department and in the eyes of the public, that what they were doing was excluding specifically single family home owners and not excluding other people.
In fact, I appeared in committee and put questions specifically to the lawyers from the Department of Justice who were there with respect to this Bill. I asked them if the wording "distribution undertaking", as amended at that committee, would catch something like a senior citizens' home. He said
September 27, 1988

yes, of course. A senior citizens' home would have to be regulated and licensed and pay fees if it had one of these dishes.
I asked similarly if it would catch a hotel and that sort of thing. Again, that was the same story. There has been this effort to clarify it, but in so clarifying it, it has reinforced the discriminatory aspect of the Bill.
In fact, it is interesting to note that in dealing with this Bill and in seeking advice from the Minister as to how this Bill is going to be applied, the Minister has told me and told every condominium owner who has contacted her in this regard, "Have no fear about this Bill. You will be excluded from this Bill by regulation".
We know, of course, that the Bill catches you and regulates you and it may license and require you to pay a fee. But she said, "Don't worry about it, because we are going to pass a regulation that will exclude you. So there is nothing to worry about".
Why is it, the condominium owners ask, if we are going to be excluded anyway by regulation, that we do not put it specifically in the Bill and say that it is quite clear, you are excluded by legislation, not by regulation?
For some reason the Minister does not seem prepared to do that. The condominium owners attribute the Minister's statement to the cable companies. They say it is because of the cable company lobby and that this country is not being run by a government of the people, by the people, for the people, but in fact it is being run by the cable companies, and it is a government of the cable companies, by the cable companies, and for the cable companies, and that in fact this sort of thing is discriminatory and a real disappointment to condominium owners across the country, and it is to me, too.

subtopic: REFUGEES-CASE OF FRANCESCO PIPERNO SENTENCED FOR TERRORISM BY ITALIAN COURT

subtopic: REFUGEES-CASE OF FRANCESCO PIPERNO SENTENCED FOR TERRORISM BY ITALIAN COURT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the abuse of Canada's immigration system by individuals who are undesirable, both in Canada and in their native countries, is becoming a major problem bordering on a serious crisis.
Adjournment Debate
Francesco Piperno, a noted Italian terrorist, successfully stayed in Canada for more than seven years. He was convicted in Italy of complicity in the murder of former Premier, Aldo Moro, in 1978. Mr. Moro was elected to office by open, democratic elections. Italy had had a democratic Government since World War II, and any changes to its society are made by the ballot box and not through violence.
The Red Brigades, of which Mr. Piperno was a member, was committed to a communist revolution to be achieved by violent means. Democracy meant nothing to these committed terrorists. Their only objective was to destroy freedom and replace it with their own notions of tyranny. The Red Brigades were noted for their terror tactics which were responsible for killing hundreds of innocent human beings.
Therefore, it is ironic that Mr. Piperno, who despised democracy, would choose the democratic system which guarantees all people freedom, to defend him from being returned to Italy to stand trial. Mr. Piperno came to Canada and claimed refugee status. The Italian Government issued a warrant for his arrest for his role in the murder of Aldo Moro, the former Italian Premier, and it attempted to extradite him in 1983. In fact, for more than seven years Mr. Piperno used all the legal means at his disposal in Canada to avoid having to return to Italy to stand trial. Mr. Piperno was even able to land a job teaching physics at the University of Alberta while he continued his fight to stay in Canada. The final irony, he applied for refugee status, refugee status in a democratic country.
Mr. Piperno's case is a celebrated one. However, this occurrence is becoming more widespread in our immigration system. Individuals with criminal records, notorious criminals, murderers, and terrorists are taking advantage of our laws to escape prosecution in their own lands.
This is not right. If an individual commits a major crime in another country, that individual must be punished in the country where the crime was committed, if he can be assured of a fair trial. Individuals cannot be allowed to circumvent justice by escaping to Canada and using our legal system to avoid punishment for their deeds. The Canadian public must be protected from these types of individuals. We Canadians are a very generous group of people who place the rights of the individual above all other commitments. Thus, we have a major quandary on our hands.
At what stage do the rights of a society supersede the rights of an individual? We must remember that the individuals with whom we are dealing are not Canadian citizens or landed immigrants. Should those individuals who are not Canadian citizens or landed immigrants be granted the same rights and access to protection of Canadians laws as are available to all Canadians? Should Canadians be allowed to foot the bill for those individuals who are deliberately using our system of justice to evade punishment for a crime committed in their native country?

September 27, 1988
Adjournment Debate
I believe that as legislators it is our duty to address this very serious problem, for it relates directly to the society we want for Canada. At present, due to the past policies of the previous Liberal Government, and the intransigent actions of the other place on Bills C-55 and C-84, our system has become inundated with false claims by individuals with unsavoury backgrounds. This, in turn, has sent out a false message to the world that, if one can get to Canada, one will have at his or her disposal all the mechanisms enjoyed by Canadian citizens and landed immigrants.
In addition, individuals who use Canada's immigration laws and legal system to escape prosecution for capital offences committed in foreign lands, create a negative impression of our system of justice. Canadians have every right to ask whether a dual system of justice is being practised. The taking of an innocent life in another country is the same as taking that life in Canada. Murder is a capital offence in all civilized societies, regardless of the political stripe of a government.
If one can escape to Canada after committing a murder, are we in effect condoning that crime, if an individual is somehow successful in staying in Canada? What if an individual who has committed a crime and has managed to escape to Canada and while using our legal system to gain status here, commits another murder? Who is responsible for the termination of an innocent life? The individual would still be alive if the perpetrator of the crime had not been allowed access into Canada and used our legal system to further his or her position. Therefore, even though the Government has passed legislation which will stop the cheaters and criminals of the world from entering Canada under false pretenses, further action is required. We need short-term measures which will prevent abuse of our immigration system until January 1, 1989 when the provisions of Bill C-55 and Bill C-84 come into effect.
Second, all individuals in Canadian jails who are fighting extradition to other countries for committing a capital offence should be sent back. Charles Ng is a prime example of an individual who committed the most heinous crimes in California and is still in Canada after four years of fighting extradition to the United States.
Third, any individual who commits terrorist acts in countries which have democratic Governments should be returned to those nations.
Fourth, all terrorists who commit crimes against innocent civilians, such as airplane hijackers, should be returned to those countries to face justice.
The message must be clear to all that Canada only wants those who are peaceful and law-abiding. Individuals who do not meet this criterion need not bother to come to Canada for they will be sent back. Canada was built by those individuals who had the greatest respect for the law. It is up to us as legislators to ensure that Canada continues this tradition. Our
democratic institutions are our greatest asset and sometimes one of our weaknesses, but the more we recognize how fragile our democratic institutions really are, the more we will do to strengthen them. I am certain that our immigration system will once again acquire a worldwide reputation of being fair and accessible by those individuals who possess all the qualities which will continue to strengthen Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Hawkes (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REFUGEES-CASE OF FRANCESCO PIPERNO SENTENCED FOR TERRORISM BY ITALIAN COURT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for following up on his question. When he asked the question in May of 1987, the Minister could not give a full and complete reply because the case was before the Immigration Appeal Board. Subsequently, Mr. Piperno voluntarily left Canada, in January of this year, and withdrew all of his legal applications.
I guess this emphasizes the reality that someone can come to Canada as a visitor and despite being convicted of a very serious offence which resulted in a ten-year sentence, remain in this country until January of this year. It emphasizes for the House and Canadians the problem with the law that was on the books prior to this Parliament's action early last fall and the Senate's subsequent concurrence in our judgment a year later. It is a bit of a shame that the Senate took so long to approve legislation passed by democratically elected members of this Chamber, and we have to live with the consequences.
I would like to pay tribute to the Hon. Member. I served with him on the Standing Committee on Employment and Immigration. He has had a longstanding interest in helping change the legislation so we could separate the true immigrant and the true refugee from those who would abuse our system. He brought to our attention a case of what he viewed to be abuse, and I am pleased to report that the law has been changed and the man in question has left the country and is currently serving his sentence in Italy.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-ESTONIA-RECOGNITION OF HONORARY CONSUL GENERAL
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-ESTONIA-RECOGNITION OF HONORARY CONSUL GENERAL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, have you been nominated as yet for the upcoming election? I am pleased to hear that. That is good. I have as well. I was nominated in a wonderful community centre in my riding called the Latvian Cultural Centre. That is really a great spot. I hope you will have an opportunity to visit it one day because it is the centre of the Latvian community in my riding and in Metropolitan Toronto. They have all sorts of Latvian cultural activities, language classes, history classes and dancing classes. I know you would enjoy them. As well, it is really a community centre for the whole neighbourhood. In fact, I have had fund raising dinners there, I think about six. I was nominated there in 1982 and again earlier this year. It is a very active place and a great spot in our community.
One of the reasons it is located there is that it attracts an awful lot of Canadians of Latvian origin who live in nearby neighbourhoods. I have a lot of Canadians of Latvian origin in
September 27, 1988

my constituency. Interestingly enough, just outside my constituency is the Estonian Cultural Centre, called Estonia House, on Broadview Avenue. As a result of that, of course, there are a lot of Estonian Canadians who live nearby as well. In addition, we have a goodly number of Lithuanian Canadians.
You are aware, Madam Speaker, that Canadians of Latvian, Estonian and Lithuanian origin are called Baltic peoples. They come from the Baltic nations, if you will, and in fact I suppose something like 2.1 per cent of all my constituents could be described as being originally from the Baltic states. I am sure you are aware, Madam Speaker, that back in the 13th century-that is quite a way back and we have to look at history-Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania were independent countries. After that they became dominated by one neighbouring country after another and lost their independence but never the goal of freedom and independence.
After the First World War in 1918, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania became once again sovereign, independent, free nations. They remained that way until the Second World War, in fact, until 1940, when the Red Army of the Soviet Union invaded them and in so doing broke three peace-keeping treaties or non-aggression pacts with those three nations. Those Baltic states were devastated by the Soviets. In fact, in one month alone in the year 1941, while the Soviet Red Army was occupying those three countries, over 100,000 people were sent off to labour camps. Thousands were imprisoned, tortured or murdered.
On top of that, in 1941 the Nazis invaded and wreaked the same sort of devastation. About 300,000 Jewish residents of those three nations were deported or executed during the Nazi occupation of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania during the Second World War.
After all that came the Yalta Conference in which Mr. Churchill, Mr. Roosevelt and Mr. Stalin got together and divided up Europe into spheres of influence, deciding that Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania should be in the Soviet sphere of influence. Immediately after that, within the next few years, with the Soviet troops again occupying those countries, something like 500,000 people of Estonian, Latvian and Lithuanian origin were deported to the Soviet Union. Between 1940 and the early 1950s about 10 per cent of the total population just disappeared, deported to the Soviet Union.
Canada recognized the independence, sovereignty and freedom of those three Baltic states, namely, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. When they were taken over and occupied by the Soviets, Canada never recognized that illegal annexation or occupation. We have always considered, as far as legalities were concerned, that those three countries should remain independent nations.
Each of those nations has an honorary Consul General here in Canada. Up until 1972, those honorary Consuls General of
Adjournment Debate
Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania here in Canada were officially recognized and listed in a publication of the Department of External Affairs called The Diplomatic Corps and Consular and Other Representatives in Canada. However, since 1972, they have not been listed in our Canadian diplomatic directory. That is not so in other countries. Lor instance, the United States and Australia officially recognize the honorary Consuls General of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania to those countries. Here in Canada, since 1972 when we dropped them from our official recognition list, we have been thinking about it and considering whether we should put them back on the list and whether we should in some way recognize them again.
It seems rather strange that for 16 years now, Canada has been thinking about this and wondering about it, and Canadians of Estonian, Latvian and Lithuanian origin and many others including me wonder if it is just that we are slow thinkers and learners in Canada. What is going on that it is taking so long, or is it really that we are lacking in courage? Is that the whole reason for it?
Recently, even Mr. Gorbachev, the Secretary General of the Soviet Union, seems to have had more courage with respect to Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania than we Canadians have had. In fact, recently Mr. Gorbachev has allowed Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania to ask publicly to be made sovereign states and have sovereign status, to have representatives at the United Nations, to have representation at the Olympics, to have control of their own press and to have control over foreign travel and their own military and secret police. He has allowed Estonia actually to set up a commission to investigate the status of the deportations.
Why is it that Mr. Gorbachev has all this courage? If Mr. Gorbachev can have all this courage, why can't Canada have the same sort of courage and recognize in our diplomatic registry the Honorary Consuls General of Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania? Why is that?

speakeroldname: Mr. Michel Champagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-ESTONIA-RECOGNITION OF HONORARY CONSUL GENERAL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first, I think that I should congratulate my colleague from York East (Mr. Redway) for the excellent presentation he has just given us on Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. I would like, perhaps, to remind his constituents that in defending them so vigorously, he shows, I think, how sensitive he is to the ethnic communities and how welcoming Canada is as a country, one that is built on such ethnic communities.
And that also is why the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) had the pleasure to reiterate in the House the policy of the Canadian Government on the Baltic States of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. He clearly stated at the outset that we have no intention to recognize de jure the occupation of these countries by the Soviet Union since 1940. However, like all Canadian Governments since that time, we recognize

September 27, 1988
Adjournment Debate
their de facto annexation, because the Soviet Union exercises its authority over this territory.
This statement of principle is based on some concrete actions. The Government continues to allow acting honorary consuls from Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania to perform their duties in Canada.
Official relations with the authorities of the Baltic States are limited. No Canadian ambassador goes to the region. Other Canadian officials who go there avoid relations with the local authorities as much as possible.
Special procedures have been established to make it easier for Baltic representatives in other countries to come to Canada in the exercise of their duties.
Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania may be shown as acceptable birthplaces on Canadian passports and immigration documents.
To reassure my colleague from York East (Mr. Redway), these measures and others show that Canada still refuses to accept Soviet control over the Baltic States, and Soviet authorities are fully aware of that.
As to the listing of Acting Honourary Consul Generals of the Baltic States in the Department of External Affairs publication entitled "The Diplomatic Corps and Consular and Other Representatives in Canada", our policy is not to delete the names already listed but not to add the names of new consuls. Successive Canadian Governments did review the question and decided to maintain this policy.
In conclusion I would say that the Minister is very much aware of the concerns voiced by Canada's Baltic community and, without losing sight of the wider consequences relating to our foreign policy, he will certainly make it a point to take them under very serious consideration on every appropriate occasion.
